posts.title: Crowdfunding’s Hamas Problem: A Gaza Fundraiser’s Telegram Badge Leads to an Al-Qassam Chat
posts.description: Two Chuffed pages raised $12,948 and $6,736 for a Gaza man whose Telegram status badge traces to a chat named for al-Qassam, Hamas’s armed wing. One organizer said the money would reach him “probably via PayPal or a crypto wallet.”
posts.body: An abstract identifier graph over a map of the Gaza Strip. No real person is depicted. Illustration: OctoProbe News; map © OpenStreetMap contributors. Do crowdfunding sites host Gaza fundraisers that carry open Hamas signals? They do, and the signals sit in plain view. Two live Chuffed campaigns have raised $12,948 and $6,736 for a Gaza man whose Telegram status badge comes from a channel that sends followers to a chat named for al-Qassam, Hamas’s armed wing. Treasury says Hamas exploits Gaza’s suffering to raise money. The photo is the same on both pages: a young man in a black cap, in profile, against a field of rubble. On Chuffed, an Australian crowdfunding site, it heads two campaigns for “Ashraf,” a 23-year-old in Gaza. As of October 20, 2026, the older page showed $12,948 raised from 192 supporters. The newer one showed $6,736 from 99. The same photo is the profile picture of the Telegram account @Ashrafgaza, which has posted links to both campaigns. That account wears a status badge from an emoji set called “Resistance-Toast.” A Telegram channel by the same name, with about 17,650 subscribers, points its readers to a group chat called “Al-Qassam Toast.” The Izz ad-Din al-Qassam Brigades are Hamas’s military wing. Neither campaign mentions Hamas. Neither shows where the money goes after it lands. Chuffed pays donations straight to an organizer’s PayPal or Stripe account, and the onward route to Gaza is the organizer’s call. One organizer told donors the money would reach Ashraf “probably via PayPal or a crypto wallet.” Editor’s note: Hamas has been a designated Foreign Terrorist Organization since October 8, 1997. Federal law punishes anyone who “knowingly provides material support or resources to a foreign terrorist organization.” Under OctoProbe’s standards, this report does not link the Telegram channel or chat described below. Key Takeaways Two Chuffed campaigns for the same Gaza man, run by organizers in the United States and Australia, showed $12,948 and $6,736 raised on October 20, 2026. Chuffed pays donations to the organizer at or around the time of each gift. One organizer said the money would move on “probably via PayPal or a crypto wallet.” The man’s Telegram status badge comes from a “Resistance-Toast” emoji set. A channel of that name steers its 17,650 subscribers to a chat called “Al-Qassam Toast.” Crowdfunding pays out in ordinary money; Hamas asks for stablecoins. FBI affidavits list a dozen wallets tied to al-Qassam fundraising and trace about 1.35 million USDT into one of them in just over four months. News reports have flagged fundraisers tied to Hamas supporters on both Chuffed and GoFundMe. Treasury says Hamas may have collected as much as $10 million a month through sham-charity donations. GoFundMe’s terms ban terrorist financing by name. Chuffed’s terms do not mention terrorism. Two Pages, One Photo The older campaign, “Help Ashraf’s Family!,” went up on April 6, 2025. Its organizer lists a location in the United States. The story, signed by Ashraf, gives his age as 20. “We have been displaced and are living in a tent in the city of Deir al-Balah,” it reads. The page asked for $15,000. It had 192 supporters and 135 shares. The April 2025 campaign on October 20, 2026. Source: Chuffed, captured October 20, 2026. The newer campaign, “Help Ashraf and his family maintain their life in Gaza,” went up on February 20, 2026, under an organizer in Australia. It asks for $10,000. “I speak for my family of 10 members,” Ashraf wrote. The organizers’ write-up says they have spoken with him weekly “For nearly three years.” The February 2026 campaign uses the same lead photo as the 2025 page. Source: Chuffed, captured October 20, 2026. The two pages are tied together three ways. They lead with the same photograph. They carry the same update, word for word, which opens, “My name is Ashraf, I’m 23 years old and living in Gaza with my family of 10.” And the Telegram account that uses that photograph as its profile picture has posted links to both. Chuffed shows each campaign’s total in the organizer’s home currency. The Australian page marks gifts in U.S. dollars separately, which indicates its $6,736 total is in Australian dollars. The two totals are not added together in this report for that reason. “Probably via PayPal or a Crypto Wallet” Chuffed does not hold the money. Its terms say PayPal and Stripe donations “will be paid to the Social Venture’s PayPal account or Stripe account at or around the time of your Donation.” Both campaign pages tell donors the organizer “will have quick and easy access to your donation.” That puts the last leg of the trip, from a Western bank account into Gaza, outside the platform’s view. The U.S. organizer spelled out the plan, writing of work with a small team to “raise money for him, and transfer it to him probably via PayPal or a crypto wallet.” The U.S. organizer’s note on the 2025 campaign. Source: Chuffed, captured October 20, 2026. Inside Gaza, Hamas runs its own financial plumbing. When the Treasury Department sanctioned a Gaza lender in October 2024, it described Al-Intaj Bank as “an unlicensed Hamas-run bank in Gaza that provides financial services for Hamas despite not being connected to international banks.” The Telegram Trail Screenshots gathered for an OctoProbe investigation show @Ashrafgaza working the campaigns hard. In a Telegram group called “Palestine Lives Matter,” which listed 1,810 members, he posted an appeal for small donations and shares with the 2026 campaign link. A search of the group returned 31 messages from him, dating back at least to December 2024. Many carry links to one of the two Chuffed pages. The same screenshots capture his profile. Telegram’s own panel says he set an emoji from “Resistance-Toast :: @fStikBot” as his current status, and labels emoji status a premium feature. Telegram’s public page for the set says only that “a Telegram user” created it. A Telegram channel carries the same name: “Resistance Toast🔻[Cyber Army].” It had about 17,650 subscribers on October 20, 2026. Its description invites readers into a group chat called “Al-Qassam Toast [Cyber Army],” which listed 3,536 members. The channel signs its posts with a red inverted triangle. From status badge to chat: (1) the @Ashrafgaza profile; (2) the “Resistance-Toast” emoji set used as his status; (3) the channel of the same name; (4) the chat its description promotes. Source: Telegram public pages, captured October 20, 2026. That triangle has a history. The Anti-Defamation League says the symbol “first appeared in propaganda videos from the al-Qassam Brigades, Hamas’s military wing, marking Israeli military targets with inverted red triangles.” The ADL also cautions that “context must be considered” because some users treat it as a general symbol of support for Palestine. What the Record Shows, and What It Doesn’t A status badge is a signal, not a membership card. No public record reviewed for this report ties Ashraf to Hamas operations, and both campaigns describe food, water, medicine, and shelter. The record also cannot say where the $12,948 and $6,736 went after they reached the organizers. What the record does show is the pattern U.S. officials warn about. “Hamas has exploited the suffering in Gaza to solicit funds through sham and front charities that falsely claim to help civilians in Gaza,” the Treasury Department said in October 2024. “As of early 2024, Hamas may have received as much as $10 million a month through such donations.” The group has also asked for money online in the open. In 2020 the Justice Department said the al-Qassam Brigades posted calls for bitcoin donations and “boasted that bitcoin donations were untraceable and would be used for violent causes.” Federal agents seized 150 cryptocurrency accounts tied to the campaign. The Conversion Cycle Crowdfunding runs on ordinary money. Hamas asks for cryptocurrency. The step that joins the two is conversion, when dollars paid out to an organizer are handed to a go-between, such as a friend, a money transfer office, or an exchange, and turned into digital tokens. After that step, a gift raised for food in Gaza looks like any other entry on a blockchain. GoFundMe bans the step outright. Its terms require organizers “Not to convert funds raised through the Platform into cryptocurrency for the purposes of delivering those funds to its intended recipients” and add that “All funds must be withdrawn and delivered in fiat currency.” Chuffed’s terms say nothing about cryptocurrency. The U.S. organizer of the 2025 Ashraf page named a crypto wallet as one likely route. On the Gaza end, crypto is one of the few ways left to get cash. Al Jazeera reported in June 2025 that with no banking services left in the territory, residents rely on exchange offices and “the option to swap cryptocurrency for physical currency.” No record reviewed for this report shows that money from either Ashraf campaign took that route or reached Hamas. Hamas has written its own instructions for the conversion step. In a 2026 affidavit, an FBI agent quoted an email that a confidential source received in February 2025 from fund[@]alqass██.██, an address the FBI ties to the al-Qassam Brigades. In the FBI’s rough translation, it told donors with no crypto experience that they could “seek the help of a friend inside or outside your country, or go to a money transfer office or exchange in your country that has digital currencies, and show only the wallet information from this message.” It added that “it is necessary not to inform the party that will undertake the transfer on your behalf of our identity.” The email supplied a USDT stablecoin address on the TRON network and warned that “the address is only valid for one transfer and support process.” The agent assessed that the network had been running since about October 2024 and had “received over $3,000,000 in donations through in or around November 2025.” As recently as February 2026, the agent wrote, the address was still emailing FBI sources instructions on how to donate. Following the Stablecoins An earlier affidavit, filed with a March 25, 2025, application to seize USDT held by Tether, traces where the donations went. Of 25,211 USDT sent to the first address an FBI source received, 23,618 USDT moved directly to a wallet the agent called the “al-Qassam Brigades Operational Wallet.” That wallet took in about 1,349,725 USDT between October 28, 2024, and March 3, 2025, according to the filing. A second source emailed the same address and received seven more donation addresses. Together they took in about 45,948 USDT between February 14 and February 28, 2025. All seven paid their transaction fees from one shared “Gas Wallet,” which the agent wrote marks them as controlled by the same actor. The agent estimated that the operational wallet “receives an average of approximately 75,000 USDT per week that is subsequently sent to finance terrorism.” Paragraph 63 of the FBI affidavit lists the seven addresses a second source received. OctoProbe masked the end of the al-Qassam domain. Source: U.S. Department of Justice. From there the trail runs back toward cash. The agent described internal “book transfers” between accounts at the same exchange, which leave no public blockchain record, and payments to a Turkish exchange. The agent wrote that regional over-the-counter brokers “can be used to obfuscate the flow of funds and swap virtual currency into government-issued fiat currency.” Tether froze the USDT in all 18 Tether addresses named in the application at the U.S. government’s request. These are the wallets an OctoProbe investigation of the fund[@]alqass██.██ address logged from the two filings, with the three additional addresses from paragraph 63: USDT address (TRON) Role in the DOJ filings In OctoProbe graph TSWL3euRjZWXiFJgzuV9tYAGiwShtPWkZK Donation Address 1, sent to the first FBI source in February 2025 Yes TA3aQxRwocYytqZBKqMPHPZT6pYvwGjLg1 Operational wallet, the network’s main consolidation point (Target Property 13) Yes TVp7a1r4FGNgWE2ViskhcfVYxbyZRvpvmv Sent to the second source (Target Property 2) No TB6PG69uKdN6NJirx8PnV7mJMVh4XRZvzp Sent to the second source (Target Property 3) Yes THeKAQbUnV58Hnt8WxwwXaC4EjzTquoVes Sent to the second source (Target Property 14) Yes TL4MeyPRooqL9UhCiqAHww7u2pNYs6guJS Sent to the second source (Target Property 15) Yes TSxBp5UrV7HDp7Zu5EJc1ijDWGWhwsfBFK Sent to the second source (Target Property 16) No TTzRqud2nVZJUSahxspmqjTHZKmfj3d9Uc Sent to the second source (Target Property 17) Yes TX8VZHoXwwGDvL75m7cZee1gyipac3p5PQ Sent to the second source (Target Property 18) No TDyyV8bkNNfttzk3NvjGvLFobsGdYmig9J Sent to a third source (Target Property 4) Yes TQaNC6oaN8TVtvbVv7vDZUAhPZrfuP76Vp Named for seizure (Target Property 5) Yes TGmLbZiS4SAhxDwmQteQ2fhsKJQ7VfJLsv Named for seizure (Target Property 12) Yes Every address above passes the TRON checksum. OctoProbe masks the final quarter of the al-Qassam Brigades’ web domain in text and images. A Pattern Across Platforms The two Ashraf pages are a small slice of a large market. In August 2025, the i Paper reported that Chuffed “has nearly 10,000 individual campaign pages for Gazans.” The paper found one of them used a real Gaza doctor’s stolen photos. Chuffed removed it after the paper asked. The company told the paper that a campaign found to be fraudulent “will be redacted and the campaigner banned from our platform.” In March 2026, the Telegraph reported that Chuffed was hosting fundraisers for people accused of supporting Hamas, among them a suspended National Health Service doctor under police investigation who had raised more than £44,000. GoFundMe faces the same problem. The Jerusalem Post reported in September 2025 that volunteer researchers tied a Gaza cleric’s €500,000 GoFundMe appeal to a member of a Hamas-affiliated preachers’ forum and found footage of a recruiter urging Gazan youth to become “Soldiers of the next October 7.” GoFundMe froze the campaign within 36 hours, the paper reported. Writer Eitan Fischberger reported on his Substack in May 2025 that a Gaza doctor who honored relatives in the al-Qassam Brigades had raised more than $40,000 on GoFundMe, and that Western platforms “are ill-equipped to stop it.” The money involved is large. GoFundMe told Al Jazeera it “has helped raise and deliver over $300m from donors in more than 215 countries and jurisdictions to support individuals and organisations helping those in both Gaza and Israel.” Charity leaders and activists quoted in the same report accused the company of shutting down or freezing Gaza fundraisers. The Rules on Paper GoFundMe’s terms prohibit “any activity in support of terrorism, terrorist financing, extremist financing, or money laundering.” Its guidance on the Israel–Gaza war adds, “Fundraising to support any armed conflict efforts is not allowed, regardless of the country.” Chuffed’s terms are vaguer. The site is run by Chuffed.org Pty Ltd under the laws of New South Wales, Australia. Its terms, last updated November 11, 2025, never use the word “terrorism.” They bar content that “breaches applicable laws, regulations or relevant industry codes, or is otherwise unlawful.” Donations on both Ashraf pages are processed by Stripe and PayPal, according to the pages themselves. How This Story Was Reported An OctoProbe investigation began with two identifiers and grew over four rounds to 33 nodes and 41 links. It connected the campaign pages, the Telegram account, nine images uploaded by the analyst, and contact points for one organizer. Reporters then captured both campaign pages and the public Telegram pages on October 20, 2026, and compared the campaigns’ lead photo with the Telegram profile photo by eye. They match. posts.title: Subpoena, Order, Warrant: How the Government Gets Your Data
posts.description: Two FOIA releases, one from House committees and one from the Navy’s criminal investigators, show what a subpoena can demand, what it can’t, and where a judge has to step in.
keywords: Committee on the Judiciary v. McGahn
posts.body: Three branches, three kinds of compulsory process. Excerpts from the two FOIA releases discussed below. Graphic: OctoProbe News. What records can Congress, a federal agency or a court force a tech company to hand over about your account? All three branches can compel records. A congressional or agency subpoena needs no judge, and served on a tech company it reaches basic subscriber records such as name, address, IP logs, device identifiers and payment data. Records of who communicated with whom, and when, need a judge’s § 2703(d) order. Message content needs a warrant based on probable cause. Key Takeaways Congress, executive agencies and the courts each compel records, under different authority and different limits. No judge signs a congressional or administrative subpoena before it goes out. A House committee subpoena reaches anything “touching matters of inquiry committed to said committee.” The courts require a valid legislative purpose, and enforcement runs through contempt or a lawsuit. An inspector general’s subpoena reaches only what its statute allows. Served on Apple, Google, Meta or Snap, it gets the basic subscriber records listed in 18 U.S.C. § 2703(c)(2): name, address, session logs, IP addresses, identifiers, payment. A § 2703(d) order, signed by a judge, works like a pen register: it shows who talked to whom, when and for how long, not what was said. Message content takes a warrant based on probable cause, and the major platforms say they hand it over only on one. Retention is often the tighter limit. In the FBI’s carrier retention chart, as of March 2019, call records lasted one to seven years and most carriers kept no text-message content at all; Verizon and U.S. Cellular kept it for days. Most federal crimes can be charged for five years. One NCIS FOIA release shows all of it in a single month: eight inspector general subpoenas to tech and telecom companies, a military judge’s subpoena, a sealed federal court subpoena and a search warrant attachment for a Kik account. Every branch of the federal government can make you hand over records. Congress does it with committee subpoenas. Executive agencies do it with administrative subpoenas that their own lawyers sign. Courts do it with grand jury subpoenas, court orders and search warrants. The three instruments look alike on paper. Each opens with a command and ends with a signature. But they rest on different constitutional footing, they answer to different standards, and they reach different things. Two Freedom of Information Act releases show the difference in the government’s own paperwork. The first is a 53-page file of seven House committee subpoenas served on the FBI in 2023, four of them on then-Director Christopher A. Wray. The second is a 35-page Naval Criminal Investigative Service release of ten subpoenas from November 2025. Most went to Apple, Google, Meta, Snap and other providers for account records. Both are posted below in full, with page images of the key passages. The documents The House file collects seven subpoenas, issued “By Authority of the House of Representatives of the Congress of the United States of America,” with their schedules, instructions and cover letters. Six came from the Committee on the Judiciary and one from the Committee on Oversight and Accountability. Five demand documents from the FBI and three of its officials were ordered to sit for depositions. The schedules range from school-board threat investigations to an FBI Richmond field office analysis of “Radical-Traditionalist Catholics,” informant forms mentioning “Biden,” and the bureau’s contacts with social media companies on content moderation. The NCIS release answers requests for “all subpoenas issued by this Service for the month of November 2025.” The agency’s letter, dated Feb. 18, 2026, and addressed to Michael Howell, says a search “resulted in locating ten subpoenas responsive to your request.” Eight are Defense Department inspector general subpoenas, one is a military judge’s subpoena to a hotel and one is a sealed federal court subpoena withheld in full. Names, email addresses, usernames and phone numbers of the people involved are blacked out under FOIA exemptions (b)(6) and (b)(7)(C). House Judiciary and Oversight Committee subpoenas to the FBI, 2023 53 pages · seven subpoenas, cover letters, schedules, instructions · scanned PDF, 3.6 MB Released under FOIA. The file carries no agency cover letter. Hosted as received, without a text layer. View PDF · Download NCIS FOIA release 2026-002860: ten subpoenas, November 2025 35 pages · release letter dated Feb. 18, 2026 · PDF, 4.2 MB Released by the Naval Criminal Investigative Service under FOIA. Redactions under (b)(6), (b)(7)(C) and (b)(7)(D) are the agency’s. View PDF · Download Editor’s note: The House file is a scanned image with no text layer; OctoProbe ran optical character recognition on every page to read it, and each quotation below was checked against the page image. The file contains no agency transmittal letter, so the releasing agency and requester cannot be confirmed from the document itself. Two proof-of-service pages appear out of order (page 2 is captioned for Thomas J. Sobocinski; page 53 for Wray). Both PDFs are hosted exactly as received. Page images were cropped and converted to grayscale; all redactions are the agencies’ own. Checksums are in the SHA256SUMS file. Where does each branch get the power to compel? Each branch draws on a different article of the Constitution. Congress’s subpoena power is implied from Article I’s grant of “legislative Powers.” Agencies have only the subpoena power a statute gives them. The courts issue process under Article III and the Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure, and only a judge can sign a search warrant. Branch Instrument Who issues Legal standard What it can reach How enforced Article I (Congress) Committee subpoena Committee chair or authorized member; attested by the clerk Must serve a valid legislative purpose and cover “matters of inquiry committed to said committee”; no judge beforehand Documents and testimony from officials, companies and private persons Criminal contempt referral (2 U.S.C. §§ 192, 194) or a civil lawsuit Article II (Executive) Administrative subpoena, e.g. an inspector general subpoena duces tecum Agency official under statute; here a DoD inspector general lawyer, at NCIS’s request Within the agency’s authority, not too indefinite, reasonably relevant (United States v. Morton Salt Co.); no judge beforehand Only what the statute allows. From a provider: the six basic subscriber categories in 18 U.S.C. § 2703(c)(2). IG subpoenas cannot compel testimony Government asks a district court for an order; defying the order is contempt of court Article III (Courts) Grand jury or trial subpoena (Fed. R. Crim. P. 17) Court clerk issues it signed and sealed; prosecutor fills it in Relevance (United States v. R. Enterprises, Inc.) Documents and testimony; from a provider, the same § 2703(c)(2) subscriber records Contempt of court Article III (Courts) § 2703(d) court order Judge “Specific and articulable facts” showing the records are “relevant and material” to an ongoing criminal investigation Metadata, the who-not-what: sender and recipient logs, email headers, call and text logs; no content Contempt; provider may move to quash if unduly burdensome Article III (Courts) Search warrant (Fed. R. Crim. P. 41; § 2703(a)) Neutral magistrate or judge, on oath Probable cause and particularity Stored content: email, messages, photos, cloud files; also anything lower tiers reach Executed by agents; provider must comply Editor’s note: Military judges can also issue subpoenas and Stored Communications Act warrants in cases under the Uniform Code of Military Justice. That system, created by Congress under Article I and run inside the Defense Department, is discussed separately below. Article I: What can a congressional subpoena demand? A congressional subpoena can demand almost anything that bears on a committee’s jurisdiction, from anyone, and no judge reviews it before it goes out. The form itself sets the scope. Each subpoena in the House file opens with the same command: “You are hereby commanded to be and appear before the Committee on the Judiciary of the House of Representatives of the United States at the place, date, and time specified below.” A checkbox then selects what is required: “to produce the things identified on the attached schedule,” “to testify at a deposition” or “to testify at a hearing,” each “touching matters of inquiry committed to said committee or subcommittee; and you are not to depart without leave of said committee or subcommittee.” The form is addressed to “The U.S. Marshals Service, or any authorized Member or congressional staff to serve and make return,” and closes: “Witness my hand and the seal of the House of Representatives of the United States, at the city of Washington, D.C.” It is signed by the “Chairman or Authorized Member” and attested by the clerk. The House Judiciary Committee’s February 2023 subpoena to the FBI director. The production box is checked; the deposition and hearing boxes are not. House subpoena file, p. 1. What a committee wants goes in the schedule. The first Wray subpoena, signed in February 2023, demanded records “from January 26, 2021 to present, in unredacted form” about the attorney general’s Oct. 4, 2021, memorandum on threats to school officials and the FBI’s “EDUOFFICIALS threat tag.” Schedule A to the February 2023 subpoena: school-board threat records, “in unredacted form.” House subpoena file, p. 3. The instructions widen the net. The subpoenas define “documents in your possession, custody or control” to include “documents that have been placed in the possession, custody, or control of any third party.” The definition of “communication” runs from email and text to “encrypted instant messaging application (e.g., Signal, WhatsApp, Telegram, etc.),” Discord, Microsoft Teams, Slack and “one-way communications channels (e.g., Teleporter).” The subpoenas’ definition of “communication” names Signal, WhatsApp and Telegram. House subpoena file, p. 8. The House also tells recipients which objections it will ignore. Under Instruction 17, “the Committee does not recognize: any purported non-disclosure privileges associated with the common law including; any purported privileges or protections from disclosure under the Freedom of Information Act; or any purported contractual privileges, such as non-disclosure agreements.” Any such “non-constitutional legal bases for withholding” are declared “of no legal force and effect” unless the committee agrees otherwise. Constitutional claims, such as executive privilege or the Fifth Amendment, are not on the list. Instruction 17(b) and (c), repeated in each document subpoena’s instructions. House subpoena file, p. 19. Testimony subpoenas use the same form with a different box checked. Two Judiciary subpoenas dated Aug. 21, 2023, ordered FBI Baltimore field office officials Thomas J. Sobocinski and Ryeshia Holley to sit for depositions in September about the Justice Department’s investigation of Hunter Biden. A testimony subpoena: the deposition box is checked. House subpoena file, p. 52. What limits a congressional subpoena? The limit is purpose. The Constitution never mentions congressional subpoenas, and the Supreme Court has read the power as implied. In McGrain v. Daugherty (1927), the Court held “that the power of inquiry—with process to enforce it—is an essential and appropriate auxiliary to the legislative function.” Thirty years later, in Watkins v. United States (1957), it added: “There is no general authority to expose the private affairs of individuals without justification in terms of the functions of the Congress.” The modern statement is Trump v. Mazars USA, LLP (2020). “Congress has no enumerated constitutional power to conduct investigations or issue subpoenas,” Chief Justice John Roberts wrote, “but we have held that each House has power ‘to secure needed information’ in order to legislate.” A subpoena is valid only if it is “related to, and in furtherance of, a legitimate task of the Congress,” and Congress “may not issue a subpoena for the purpose of ‘law enforcement,’ because ‘those powers are assigned under our Constitution to the Executive and the Judiciary.’” The committees’ cover letters are written with that test in mind. The Judiciary Committee’s April 10, 2023, letter to Wray, sent with a subpoena for the Richmond field office’s “Radical-Traditionalist Catholic” analysis, quotes the Court’s description of oversight as “broad and indispensable,” cites Mazars in a footnote and lists possible bills: “legislation to prescribe how federal law-enforcement entities investigate constitutionally protected activity.” It says the subpoena was issued “in light of your disregard of our earlier voluntary requests.” The cover letter for the April 2023 subpoena. House subpoena file, p. 11. The legislative-purpose paragraph, citing Trump v. Mazars in its footnote. House subpoena file, p. 13. Schedule A to the April 2023 subpoena. House subpoena file, p. 16. The Oversight Committee’s May 3, 2023, letter claims “broad authority to investigate ‘any matter’ at ‘any time’ under House Rule X” and says the subpoena “is issued pursuant to my authority as the Chairman of the Committee pursuant to both Rule XI.2(m)(1)(B) of the Rules of the House of Representatives and Rule 12(g) of the Committee’s rules.” Its schedule has one line: “All FD-1023 forms, including within any open, closed, or restricted access case files, created or modified in June 2020, containing the term ‘Biden.’” The Oversight Committee chairman cites the House rule that lets him sign subpoenas. House subpoena file, p. 25. The one-item schedule to the Oversight Committee’s May 2023 subpoena. House subpoena file, p. 28. The Judiciary Committee’s Aug. 17, 2023, subpoena reached the FBI’s dealings with tech platforms. It demanded, from Jan. 1, 2020, “All documents and communications referring or relating to the moderation, deletion, suppression, restriction, or reduced circulation of content,” and all records on “alleged ‘misinformation,’ ‘disinformation,’ or ‘malinformation.’” The cover letter said the FBI’s “response without compulsory process has, to date, been woefully inadequate.” Schedule A to the August 2023 subpoena on content moderation. House subpoena file, p. 34. How does Congress enforce a subpoena? In practice, Congress relies on the other two branches to enforce its subpoenas. The criminal route is a contempt referral. Under 2 U.S.C. § 192, a summoned witness who “willfully makes default” is guilty of a misdemeanor, punishable by a fine of $100 to $1,000 and one to 12 months in jail. Under § 194, the speaker certifies the failure to the U.S. attorney, “whose duty it shall be to bring the matter before the grand jury for its action.” That puts an executive-branch prosecutor in charge of enforcing a subpoena that is often aimed at the executive branch. The civil route is a lawsuit. In Committee on the Judiciary v. McGahn, the full D.C. Circuit held in August 2020 “that the Committee has Article III standing to seek enforcement in federal court of its duly issued subpoena in the performance of constitutional responsibilities.” That did not end the case. A panel later ruled the committee had no cause of action; the full court agreed to rehear that question, and the dispute was settled in 2021, when former White House counsel Donald McGahn sat for a closed-door transcribed interview. The litigation took nearly two years. Can Congress subpoena your email? The House subpoenas in this file went to the FBI for the FBI’s records. Whether a committee can compel Google or Meta to produce a private user’s account data is a harder question, and the Stored Communications Act does not answer it cleanly. posts.title: Inside the FBI’s CAST Guide: How Carriers and Agents Pin Down a Cell Phone
posts.description: A 2019 FBI field guide, a public NDCAC briefing and an FCC order show how a phone can be made to reveal where it is, how precise the answer is, and where the law steps in.
posts.body: How a phone is narrowed down: three sectors and three round-trip range bands overlap in one spot. Illustration: OctoProbe News. The street grid is fictional. How do police and the FBI locate a cell phone, and what legal rules apply? A phone tells its carrier where it is every time the network reaches it, and investigators can trigger that on demand with an invisible “silent” message, a call that never rings or a carrier “ping.” The answer can be as rough as a tower sector or as tight as a GPS fix. Historical records generally need a warrant under Carpenter v. United States; real-time pinging is a separate, unsettled category. Key Takeaways A phone checks in through a specific tower and sector whenever the network reaches it, and carriers log those events. Investigators can trigger check-ins on demand. The FBI’s 2019 CAST guide describes a carrier “ping” that sends “a silent message” and, for one carrier, a call “without a ring.” Location gets narrowed by exclusion: a 120-degree sector, a round-trip distance band and readings from three or more towers. A GPS-based ping can be tighter still. Carpenter v. United States (2018) generally requires a warrant for historical cell-site records. The Court left real-time tracking and tower dumps undecided. A tower hit is not proof of presence. The guide itself warns that some coordinates are “NOT GPS-based” and that CAST does not testify to the accuracy of one carrier’s data. Your phone is not hiding from the cell network. To deliver a call or a text, the network has to find it, and every time it does, the phone checks in through a particular antenna on a particular tower. Carriers record those check-ins. Investigators can read them later or, with the right paperwork, cause new ones on demand. How that works, in the government’s own words, is laid out in three public documents. The first is a 139-page FBI field guide from 2019. The second is a 2018 briefing from the Justice Department’s National Domestic Communications Assistance Center (NDCAC). The third is the 2005 Federal Communications Commission order that extended federal wiretap-assistance rules to broadband. All three are posted below, with page images of the key passages. The documents The FBI guide is the “Cellular Analysis & Geo-Location Field Resource Guide,” produced by the bureau’s Cellular Analysis Survey Team and marked “Current as of March 2019.” The nonprofit Property of the People obtained it under the Freedom of Information Act, and Motherboard reported on it in October 2021. It is a training deck: how towers work, what each carrier keeps and for how long, what legal process to use, and how to plot records on a map. The CAST mission, per the guide, “is to support FBI, along with state, local, and tribal investigations through the analysis of cellular call detail records (CDRs) and their associated tower information.” Its listed priorities are, in order, “An immediate threat to life,” FBI priorities “to include National Security, Criminal, and Cyber,” and “Assistance to state, local, and other federal agencies.” The program had 5 headquarters supervisors, 15 “National Assets” embedded in field offices, and “over 50 CAST certified ‘Field Assets’” who work cases in their own offices. The FBI still advertises free CAST training for police, where students install “the FBI provided mapping software CASTViz.” CAST’s mission, priorities and staffing. FBI CAST field guide, p. 5. Handling marking redacted by OctoProbe. The NDCAC briefing is a 14-slide “Program Update” presented by then-Director Marybeth Paglino to the center’s Executive Advisory Board on April 11, 2018, at a meeting announced in the Federal Register as open to the public. NDCAC posts it on its own public site, at ndcac.fbi.gov. The FCC order is FCC 05-153, adopted Aug. 5, 2005, which applied the Communications Assistance for Law Enforcement Act (CALEA) to broadband and internet phone providers. FBI CAST, Cellular Analysis & Geo-Location Field Resource Guide 139 pages · “Current as of March 2019” · PDF, 13 MB Released under FOIA to Property of the People. Five pages carry OctoProbe redactions of personal information. View PDF · Download NDCAC Program Update, April 11, 2018 14 slides · PDF, 0.7 MB Public briefing posted by NDCAC at ndcac.fbi.gov. Unaltered. View PDF · Download FCC 05-153, CALEA and Broadband Access and Services First Report and Order, Aug. 5, 2005 · 59 pages · PDF, 0.3 MB Published FCC order. Unaltered copy of the file NDCAC hosts. View PDF · Download Editor’s note: The FBI guide’s pages carry the handling marking “UNCLASSIFIED//LES.” OctoProbe removed it from the page images in this article; it remains in the hosted PDF as released. In the hosted PDF, OctoProbe redacted a special agent’s name on page 14 and telephone numbers, an MSISDN and IMSI/IMEI columns in sample carrier records on pages 95, 111, 112 and 128. Those five pages are replaced with redacted images; every other page is as released. The NDCAC briefing is byte-identical to the copy on ndcac.fbi.gov. The FCC order is byte-identical to the copy NDCAC hosts at ndcac.fbi.gov/file-repository/34.pdf. Checksums are in the SHA256SUMS file. How a phone gives away where it is A switched-on phone is always listening. The FBI guide puts it plainly: “A cellular phone is regularly surveying the Radio Frequency (RF) environment of the cellular provider to identify the cell tower and sector with the BEST RF Signal.” The phone keeps a running list of neighboring sectors and their signal strengths, and it camps on the strongest one. A phone keeps measuring nearby sectors and camps on the strongest. FBI CAST field guide, p. 17. Handling marking redacted by OctoProbe. Each tower is usually split into sectors, and each sector has its own identifier. According to the guide, a typical “3-sector tower” transmits “through 3 separate sectors each covering approximately 120 degrees,” and each base station’s Global Cell ID “is unique on the network and not duplicated (like a fingerprint).” When the phone does something on the network, the carrier writes it down: “When a cell phone connects to a tower to conduct an outgoing call or receive an incoming call, the phone company (provider) maintains a record of that EVENT in the Call Detail Records.” A three-sector tower splits its coverage into wedges of about 120 degrees. FBI CAST field guide, p. 30. Handling marking redacted by OctoProbe. Each sector has a network-unique cell identifier; carriers format it differently. FBI CAST field guide, p. 16. Handling marking redacted by OctoProbe. So the basic unit of cell-site location information (CSLI) is a time stamp, a tower and a sector: a pie wedge, not a point. Everything else in the guide is about making that wedge smaller or making the phone produce more of them. Making a phone talk: silent texts and calls that never ring A phone that sits idle produces few records. One that’s told to answer produces them on command. The best-known trigger is the “silent SMS.” The 3GPP standard for text messaging, TS 23.040, defines a “Short Message Type 0” in its protocol-identifier field. The standard’s conformance requirement, as quoted in a 3GPP test specification change, reads: “When a mobile terminated message is type 0, the UE shall acknowledge receipt of the short message to the SC but shall discard its contents.” The phone “shall not indicate the receipt of the type 0 short message to the user,” and “the short message shall neither be stored in the (U)SIM nor ME.” In other words, the phone must answer but must not tell its owner. To deliver the message, the network first has to find the handset; the 3GPP test sequence for a Type 0 message begins with the phone’s “PAGING RESPONSE.” That round trip happens over a specific cell, and it leaves the same kind of network record a real text would. Editor’s note: 3GPP specifications are revised by release; the Type 0 language quoted here is from the conformance test text, which cites “3GPP TS 23.040, 9.2.3.9” as its reference. OctoProbe did not test how any particular carrier logs Type 0 deliveries. The FBI guide doesn’t use the term “Type 0,” but it describes the same idea in carrier products. On Sprint’s GPS “Ping,” the guide says: “A Ping is conducted with the assistance of the cellular provider. A silent message is sent to the phone requesting a location update. The phone uses its own GPS receiver and reports its location.” From the guide’s slide on Sprint’s GPS “Ping.” FBI CAST field guide, p. 100. For a carrier without that service, the guide offers a cruder trigger. Its provider table says of U.S. Cellular: “No. However, you can force a call without a ring to the target device to determine tower/sector.” The retention chart repeats it under real-time (“Prospective”) tools: “No, but force ‘no ring’ call.” The guide’s provider table. Bottom right: a call “without a ring.” FBI CAST field guide, p. 57. And for T-Mobile, the guide supplies the wording to put in a court order or warrant: “Such service provider shall initiate a signal to determine the location of the subject’s mobile device on the service provider’s network or with such other reference points as may be reasonably available and at such intervals and times as directed by the law enforcement agent serving this order.” Suggested order language for T-Mobile’s locator. FBI CAST field guide, p. 109. Anything that makes the network reach the phone (a call, a text of any kind, a data session) can produce a location record. The guide’s retention chart lists separate “Cell Site (Voice),” “Cell Site (SMS)” and “Cell Site (Data)” records for each carrier. A silent text or no-ring call just does it without the owner seeing anything. App push notifications are a different category. Sen. Ron Wyden wrote in December 2023 that governments had sought push records from Apple and Google, which hold metadata “detailing which app received a notification and when, as well as the phone and associated Apple or Google account to which that notification was intended to be delivered.” That is account data at a tech company, not tower data at a carrier. Germany is one of the few places that counts silent texts publicly. In a March 2023 answer to lawmakers, the federal government reported that the Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA) registered 37,064 “Stille SMS” in the first half of 2022 and 14,886 in the second. The Federal Police sent 12,475 and 7,228, plus 457 and 903 through outside firms. Figures for the domestic intelligence service and customs were classified “VS – Geheim.” The government cited a Federal Court of Justice ruling placing the practice under section 100i of the criminal procedure code. From a wedge to a dot: timing, triangulation and exclusion A sector wedge can cover miles. Three techniques shrink it. Distance from the tower. Carriers measure how long a signal takes to make the round trip. The guide’s explanation of Sprint’s Per Call Measurement Data (PCMD): “By using the data transfer rate between the cellular device and the tower, the cellular provider can approximate the signal distance between the tower and the cellular device using a Round Trip Delay measurement from the tower.” Verizon’s version, the Real Time Tool, provides “sector/tower and distance from tower with confidence rating.” T-Mobile’s is called True Call. The output is an arc: a band at a certain distance inside the wedge. Round-trip delay turns a sector into a distance band. FBI CAST field guide, p. 97. Handling marking redacted by OctoProbe. Multiple towers. Measuring the same signal at several towers gives intersecting arcs. The guide’s slide on T-Mobile’s E-911 Locator and AT&T’s Mobile Locator says: “TOA positioning method is based on measuring the Time of Arrival (TOA) or (Timing Advance) of a known signal sent from the cell phone and received at three or more measurement units (towers).” Its provider table describes T-Mobile’s version as “3 to 6 tower triangulation.” The sample response on the slide gives a latitude, a longitude and “Uncertainty 443 m.” Triangulation from three or more towers. The coordinates are the guide’s sample. FBI CAST field guide, p. 58. Handling marking redacted by OctoProbe. The phone’s own GPS. The Sprint ping asks the handset for a satellite fix, which the guide says depends “upon the phone interacting with a minimum of 4 satellites (3 without altitude).” For 911 calls, federal rules set the bar: handset-based systems must deliver “50 meters for 67 percent of calls, and 150 meters for 80 percent of calls,” on a per-county or per-PSAP basis. The narrowing works by exclusion. The phone is in this sector, not the other two. It is about 0.8 miles out, not 0.2 or 2. Three towers’ arcs overlap here and nowhere else. Investigators apply the same logic across many phones with “tower dumps,” lists of every device that used a site during a window. The guide suggests narrowing a tower dump “based on knowledge (outgoing call only, 3 minute conversation, not in area after crime, etc.)” Tower dumps, and how the guide suggests narrowing them. FBI CAST field guide, p. 60. Handling marking redacted by OctoProbe. Even a failed ping says something. The guide’s list of T-Mobile locator responses includes “[Absent_Subscriber] – phone is not on the network” and “[Position_Method_ Failure] – phone is powered off or has moved into an area where switch is not provisioned,” with the note: “If you see this – it may come back on.” What the locator returns, including failures. The sample phone number was redacted by OctoProbe. FBI CAST field guide, p. 111. Handling marking redacted by OctoProbe. AT&T’s historical tool, NELOS, grades each location record on a 14-step scale, from “Location accuracy likely better than 25 meters” for GPS-derived events to “better than 25000 meters” for tower-and-sector-only records. Its timing records cover cases where “low propagation delay indicates very near presence to a particular cell tower (within 200M).” AT&T’s NELOS accuracy key runs from 25 meters to 25 kilometers. FBI CAST field guide, p. 82. Handling marking redacted by OctoProbe. Real-time pinging and historical records are different things The guide separates two kinds of data, and the law increasingly does too. Historical records already exist in the carrier’s files: call detail records with cell sites, tower dumps, and engineering data such as PCMD, RTT, True Call and NELOS. The March 2019 retention chart shows AT&T keeping call records, cell sites and tower dumps for “7 years,” T-Mobile for “2 years,” Sprint for “18 months,” and Verizon for “1 year.” Engineering data is short-lived: Verizon RTT “8 days,” Sprint PCMD “~90 days SMS & voice; 2 weeks data,” AT&T NELOS “90 days.” Real-time (“prospective”) location is generated on request: AT&T’s “Mobile Locate (Triangulation / AGPS),” T-Mobile’s “E911 (Triangulation),” Sprint’s “GPS ‘Ping’ (device dependent),” and, for U.S. Cellular, the no-ring call. Verizon RTT, the guide says, is “provided to law enforcement during exigent circumstances or if requested in a legal document.” Retention periods and real-time (“prospective”) tools by carrier, as of March 2019. FBI CAST field guide, p. 74. Handling marking redacted by OctoProbe. Verizon’s Real Time Tool adds distance from the tower. FBI CAST field guide, p. 130. Handling marking redacted by OctoProbe. Retention figures are as of March 2019. Sprint has since merged into T-Mobile, and carriers’ practices may have changed. What the law requires Two kinds of court paper come up again and again in the FBI guide: a court order under 18 U.S.C. § 2703(d) and a search warrant. posts.title: Iran Says It Rules Hormuz. Its “Mine Strike” Stories Keep Falling Apart.
posts.description: The Revolutionary Guards say a rule-breaking supertanker hit one of their mines near Hormuz on Oct. 20. They named no ship, no one outside Iran has confirmed it, and their last version of the story matched descriptions of a tanker hit by a projectile at anchor inside the Gulf.
posts.body: The IRGC Navy’s “Management of the Strait of Hormuz” title card from its Oct. 20, 2026, video, over a map of the strait. Title card shown for reporting; illustration: OctoProbe Investigations, map © OpenStreetMap contributors. No one outside Iran has confirmed it. On Oct. 20, 2026, the Revolutionary Guards said a “violating” supertanker hit a mine south of the Strait of Hormuz, but they named no ship and gave no position. Maritime authorities logged no such strike, and a U.S. Central Command spokesman called Tehran’s mine claims false. Iran’s Revolutionary Guards want the world to believe they run the Strait of Hormuz. On Tuesday they ran another advertisement. The Guards’ navy said a “violating” supertanker hauling “more than 2 million barrels of crude oil” had switched off “all its radar and navigation systems,” ignored its warnings and tried to slip out by “the unauthorized southern route of the Strait of Hormuz.” Then, the Guards said, it hit a sea mine and caught fire. Tasnim News Agency was reporting the strike by 10:38 a.m. Eastern, according to the Newsquawk headline feed; the Tasnim Telegram post quoted here bears a 12:49 p.m. edit stamp (Tasnim; Newsquawk). The point came at the end. “Owners and crews of vessels in the Persian Gulf and Sea of Oman,” the Guards said, are “responsible” for using unauthorized routes, and “any movement that disregards the security of this strait will be dealt with decisively.” Strip away the packaging and little is left. Every account of the strike traces back to the Guards or to Iranian state media. The Guards named no vessel and gave no position. The only tanker incident maritime authorities logged around that time happened more than 400 nautical miles away, in the Arabian Sea. And a U.S. Central Command spokesman called Tehran’s latest mine claims false that morning. Until someone outside Iran confirms it, Tuesday’s “mine strike” is best read as propaganda. The Guards’ own record backs that reading. Ten days earlier they told nearly the same story. The next morning, Iran’s English-language Tehran Times described that ship in terms others were using for one real tanker, GEM NO.2. But GEM NO.2 had been hit by a projectile while riding at anchor inside the Gulf, about 70 nautical miles from the strait. And a tanker video Iranian outlets pushed with a similar claim in the days before turned out to be more than seven months old. Editor’s note: The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps was designated a Foreign Terrorist Organization by the secretary of state on April 8, 2019. In the Matter of the Designation of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (and Other Aliases) as a Foreign Terrorist Organization, 84 Fed. Reg. 15,278 (Apr. 15, 2019); see also U.S. Department of State, “Foreign Terrorist Organizations.” Editor’s note: The Tasnim post is in Persian; quotations are OctoProbe’s translation. The original reads, in part, «این سوپر نفتکش با بیش از 2 میلیون بشکه نفت خام، تمامی سامانه های راداری و ناوبری خود را خاموش کرده…» Key Takeaways The IRGC Navy said Oct. 20 that a “violating” supertanker hit a mine south of the Strait of Hormuz. It named no ship and gave no position, and every account traces back to Iranian sources. UKMTO logged no Oct. 20 strike in the strait. Its only tanker report around then placed an incident more than 400 nautical miles away, off Oman, and a CENTCOM spokesman called Iran’s mine claims false. The Guards told nearly the same story on Oct. 10. Tehran Times described that ship in terms then used for GEM NO.2, a supertanker hit by a projectile at anchor inside the Gulf on Oct. 9, not by a mine on a Hormuz route. A tanker video that Iranian outlets, including Tasnim and Fars, circulated amid the Guards’ Oct. 17 and 18 claims was footage from March 1, according to the fact-checking site Misbar. No earlier copy of the Oct. 20 footage has been found. It matches none of seven earlier clips checked, and the ship in it remains unidentified. What is the IRGC’s “Management of the Strait of Hormuz” brand? It is a branded video series, and the title is the claim. The clip that accompanied Tuesday’s statement opens on a yellow-and-black card reading «مدیریت تنگه هرمز», “Management of the Strait of Hormuz.” It is dated «۲۸ مهر ماه ۱۴۰۵», the Persian-calendar date for Tuesday, Oct. 20, 2026. It closes on the IRGC emblem over a Qur’anic verse: “And prepare against them whatever you are able of power” (8:60, Sahih International translation). Title card of the Oct. 20 IRGC Navy video (≈0:00). The headline reads “Management of the Strait of Hormuz”; the date line, 28 Mehr 1405, is Oct. 20, 2026. Image: IRGC Navy, via Telegram (Shabab al-Islam), shown for reporting. The same title card, caption box and emblem outro frame at least four earlier IRGC Navy tanker claims posted to the Guards’ official Sepah News site between Oct. 10 and Oct. 17, Tehran time (Sepah News 39345; 39376; 39377; 39716). It works like a recurring television segment in which Tehran polices a waterway it does not legally control. Sometimes the Guards drop the subtext. “The Strait of Hormuz is closed,” the IRGC Navy declared in a release dated Oct. 17 in Tehran, the evening of Oct. 16 in Washington (Sepah News 39716). Editor’s note: Original: «تنگه هرمز بسته است». OctoProbe translation. How often have the Guards told this story? Often enough that the words are recycled, too. Tuesday’s statement repeats phrasing the Guards have used again and again since late summer (Sepah News dates, Tehran time): “More than 2 million barrels of crude”: Oct. 17, twice (Sepah News 39716; 39740). Two million barrels is the round-number load of a very large crude carrier. It fits any supertanker. Positioning, radar and navigation systems “switched off”: Oct. 10, Oct. 11, Oct. 17 and Oct. 18 (39345; 39376; 39716; 39846). An “unauthorized” or “illegal” route south of the strait: Aug. 31, Oct. 11 and Oct. 18 (37157; 39376; 39846). Each element does narrative work. The ship went dark, so it was sneaking. It took the southern route, near Oman, so it was defying Tehran. It was big and laden, so the punishment was spectacular. And a claim that a ship was running dark can’t be checked unless someone names the ship. The Guards never do. Who is the threat aimed at? Shipowners, managers, charterers and insurers: the people who decide whether a tanker sails. Tuesday’s statement puts “owners and crews” on notice. Earlier versions went further. Any ship in the strait that switches off its navigation and identification systems “will be identified as hostile” and dealt with “severely and decisively” (Sepah News 39376; 39846). Editor’s note: Original (Sepah News 39376): «به عنوان متخاصم شناسایی و با آن به شدت و قاطعیت برخورد خواهد شد». OctoProbe translation. Who amplified the claim? The message moved through state media, the militia ecosystem and the wires within hours. Tasnim News Agency’s Telegram post of the IRGC Navy statement, stamped as edited at 12:49 p.m. Eastern on Oct. 20, 2026. The still is a crop of the video’s wide shot. Source: Tasnim, Telegram, captured Oct. 20, 2026. Time (Eastern) Outlet What Views (as of 3:05 p.m.) ~5:30 a.m. Iran International Reports an earlier IRGC “two tankers” claim n/a 10:38 a.m. Newsquawk (citing Tasnim) One “violating” tanker on fire in the southern corridor n/a 10:40 a.m. Newsquawk (CENTCOM spokesman) Mine claims “false” n/a By 12:13 p.m. Sepah News (via AFP) “Two violating oil tankers were set ablaze and halted” n/a 12:49 p.m. (edit stamp) Tasnim, Telegram One “supertanker,” 2 million-plus barrels; still image 6,570 12:56 p.m. Shabab al-Islam (“Youth of Islam”), Telegram Arabic translation plus 25-second IRGC video 94 12:59 p.m. Reuters via Devdiscourse “Supertanker” hit mine n/a 1:20 p.m. Tanjug via B92 CENTCOM, via Al Jazeera: claims “not true”; strait open n/a 1:39 p.m. TASS Same, citing Tasnim n/a Shabab al-Islam (t.me/shabab_alislam/67404) is an Arabic-language board whose bio calls it «وحدة الإعلام الحربي لأصحاب الكهف», the “War Media Unit of Ashab al-Kahf.” Its feed on Tuesday mixed Iraqi banking notices, Houthi “military media” releases and statements from Iranian commanders (channel preview). The Hormuz post carried no “forwarded from” tag. The video was re-uploaded, and the translation carried the Guards’ line to an Arabic-speaking audience. Shabab al-Islam’s re-upload of the IRGC video with an Arabic translation of the statement, posted at 12:56 p.m. Eastern. Source: Shabab al-Islam, Telegram, captured Oct. 20, 2026. Fewer than a hundred views is a modest audience. That isn’t the point. The relay turns one unverified IRGC claim into something that looks like a chorus. What do maritime authorities say happened? Nothing like what the Guards described. The U.K. Maritime Trade Operations center, the Royal Navy-run desk that merchant masters report to, published one tanker report Tuesday. Advisory 178-26 reads, in full: “UKMTO has received a report of an incident involving a tanker and military forces approximately 121NM east of Duqm, Oman. Reports indicate that the tanker was subject to interaction as part of ongoing military activity in the region. Authorities are aware and relevant investigations remain ongoing. Vessels are advised to consider the latest maritime security information and maintain awareness of the evolving operational environment.” (UKMTO; PDF) The PDF puts the incident at 1000 UTC on Oct. 19 (6 a.m. Eastern), more than a day before the Guards’ claim, and rates the source “Verified.” The EU-backed Maritime Security Centre–Indian Ocean placed it “in the Arabian Sea” (MSCIO Advisory 09-2026). Duqm itself is more than 400 nautical miles from the narrows of Hormuz, and a point 121 nautical miles east of it is farther still. The report describes “interaction” with “military forces,” not a mine. UKMTO used nearly identical language earlier this month for Advisory 163-26, “an incident involving a tanker and military forces in the Gulf of Oman.” Its weekly summary ties that entry to OCEAN MOLICA, which it lists as general cargo, and to a Central Command report that U.S. forces had disabled a ship that “attempted to run the on going naval blockade” (UKMTO VRA overview, Oct. 16). Editor’s note: Great-circle distances were measured to a reference point in the Hormuz narrows at 26.6° N, 56.4° E. Duqm port (19.67° N, 57.71° E) is about 422 nautical miles from that point; a point projected 121 nautical miles due east of the port (about 19.7° N, 59.9° E) is about 458. UKMTO’s map graphic shades an area nearer the coast, so the incident position is approximate. UKMTO’s incident list, going back to Sept. 28, holds no Oct. 20 report from the strait. None of its entries describes a mine. Every strike it logged inside the strait over that period is blamed on an “unknown” or “unidentified” projectile (UKMTO). The silence is not proof on its own. UKMTO’s weekly summary says it is “struggling to accurately report true number of attacks with majority of vessels attacked refusing to report” (UKMTO VRA overview, Oct. 16). But the Guards’ claim has no independent support. Central Command was blunter. A spokesman called Iran’s claims about tankers hitting mines false, and the Newsquawk feed carried his words in English: “We have cleared the international waterways in the Strait of Hormuz of mines” (Newsquawk). Serbia’s Tanjug news agency and China’s CGTN reported that the remarks were made to Al Jazeera; CGTN’s rendering reads “international passages” (B92/Tanjug; CGTN). According to Tanjug, the spokesman also said 95 percent of vessels are getting through the strait despite Tehran’s claims that it is closed, and called the attacks on shipping a sign of the IRGC’s “desperation” under the U.S. blockade (B92/Tanjug). Editor’s note: Tanjug reported the 95 percent figure and the “desperation” remark in Serbian (“95 odsto plovila uspešno prolazi kroz moreuz, uprkos tvrdnjama Teherana da je zatvoren”; “očaj”); the English renderings are OctoProbe’s. No English-language transcript of the spokesman’s remarks from Central Command or Al Jazeera was found. Traffic is undeniably down. A joint maritime advisory earlier this month cited independent tracking showing transits in the “single-digit numbers,” against U.S. figures of about 29 a day (JMIC Advisory Note, Oct. 11). But suppression by force is not the orderly “management” the Guards are selling. Iran, the spokesman said per Tanjug, uses “missiles and drones” in its attacks. CENTCOM’s denial was on the Newsquawk feed by 10:40 a.m. Eastern. According to Tanjug, it answered Iran’s claim that two tankers had hit mines, made in an IRGC statement earlier that day that said two “violating oil tankers were set ablaze and halted” (AFP via The Hindu; Iran International). Tehran hasn’t said whether the afternoon “supertanker” is one of those two or a third ship. What happened the last time the Guards told this story? It fell apart. On Saturday, Oct. 10, the Guards issued the claim they would repeat on Tuesday. “Statement No. 19,” posted on Sepah News at 8:17 p.m. Tehran time (12:47 p.m. Eastern), said a “violating supertanker carrying crude oil,” which “intended to exit via the unauthorized route of the Strait of Hormuz,” had suffered “a violent explosion” after hitting a sea mine. The ship had “switched off its navigation and positioning systems,” the Guards said, and its fire was “clearly visible” to people on the coast. “A horrific fire is the fate of every violating tanker that seeks to ignore the security and rules of the Strait of Hormuz” (Sepah News 39345). The release carried a branded video of a burning hull shot from the air. Anadolu Agency’s account of the statement added a “southern route” and described the ship as “capable of carrying around 2 million barrels of oil” (Anadolu Agency). The next morning, Tehran Times added a detail for English-language readers: “Maritime cargo-tracking sources say the supertanker that exploded last night while attempting an unauthorized passage through the Strait of Hormuz was carrying 2 million barrels of Saudi crude oil.” (Tehran Times, X) The post went up at 7:44 a.m. Eastern on Oct. 11. Its 4-second clip is a cut from the Guards’ Oct. 10 video. The Tehran Times clip (left) is a cut of the IRGC’s Oct. 10 video (center). Neither matches the Oct. 20 video (right). Images: Tehran Times, X; IRGC Navy via Sepah News and Telegram. Comparison: OctoProbe Investigations. Editor’s note: The Tehran Times clip (848 by 464 pixels, 3.6 seconds) was compared frame by frame against the Sepah News Oct. 10 video and matches the segment at about 18 seconds. Neither matches any frame of the Oct. 20 clip. That description matched what was being said that week about one real ship: GEM NO.2, a Panama-flagged supertanker that Reuters reported was “fully laden with oil” when it was struck (gCaptain). Later on Oct. 11, an X account described GEM NO.2 as “reportedly carrying around 2 million barrels of Saudi crude” (see below). Tehran Times did not name the ship. The facts about GEM NO.2 don’t fit the Guards’ story. The tanker wasn’t running a route. It was riding at anchor off the UAE coast, inside the Gulf, about 70 nautical miles southwest of the narrows. It wasn’t hit on Saturday night. It was hit on Friday, Oct. 9, at about 1000 GMT, roughly 31 hours before the Guards’ release. And no one outside Iran says it hit a mine. UKMTO recorded an “unknown projectile” 13 nautical miles west of Al Jazeera, UAE, without naming the ship; the Joint Maritime Information Center’s next advisory identified that incident as GEM NO.2, “at anchor in UAE TTW” (UKMTO; JMIC Advisory Note, Oct. 11). India’s shipping minister said the ship “was subjected to a drone attack at Sharjah Anchorage” (The Hindu). UKMTO said the fire was extinguished. The UAE’s WAM news agency reported that the coast guard rescued 22 crew members from a tanker fire on Oct. 10, according to All India Radio, which tied that rescue to GEM NO.2 (All India Radio). posts.description: A seven-step guide to finding an agency’s SharePoint, naming a custodian and requesting web logs, documents and Teams messages under FOIA, with Secret Service records as the worked example.
posts.body: U.S. Secret Service headquarters at 950 H St. NW in Washington. Illustration: OctoProbe News; map © OpenStreetMap contributors; Secret Service star: U.S. Secret Service. Use of the star does not imply endorsement. How do you request a federal official’s browser history, SharePoint files or Teams messages under FOIA? Find the agency’s real Microsoft 365 systems with public DNS and Microsoft’s sign-in metadata, name a custodian by name and title, and ask for each record type by the system that holds it. Results vary. The Secret Service processed requests for five senior officials’ browser histories and released records in part, but a federal appeals court has held that browsing histories an agency neither keeps nor uses are not agency records. What you can request Browser history and web-proxy, gateway, DNS or endpoint logs SharePoint and OneDrive documents a custodian created or edited Teams chats (Exchange Online mailbox), channel posts (team mailbox), channel files (SharePoint) and chat files (OneDrive) Agency card statements A sitemap of the agency’s SharePoint You can ask a federal agency for an official’s web activity, the files the official made and the chats the official sent. Requests for those records can come back empty when they don’t name the system, the person or the place the data lives. This guide fixes that in seven steps, with copy-paste language for each record. The method is a loop. Public internet records tell you where an agency keeps its files. A records request names those systems and a custodian. Each release then hands you new names, offices and systems for the next request. The worked example throughout is two rounds of requests to the U.S. Secret Service, in 2023 and 2025. Here is what one page of the first round looks like. Example The page that started this guide The page is a printout of a computer log. Each row has a timestamp, a username that begins “ron.rowe” and a box stamped “(b)(6); (b)(7)(C)” where something else used to be. Fifteen rows at 2:16 p.m. on Oct. 10, 2023, list Microsoft 365 servers, among them unitedstatessecretservice.sharepoint.com. The rest, logged between 10:33 and 10:38 p.m. on Oct. 4, list the Daily Mail, the New York Post and a run of advertising exchanges. The user was Ronald L. Rowe Jr., who had been the agency’s deputy director since April 2023, according to the Homeland Security Department. He went on to run the agency as acting director after Kimberly Cheatle resigned in July 2024. A federal law-enforcement agency treated a senior official’s web activity as a record it could search, review and release. Primary record · photographed pageOne page of a deputy director’s web log What the page shows Dates. 15 rows at 10/10/2023 14:16; the rest between 10/4/2023 22:33 and 22:38, newest first. User. A username column that begins ron.rowe. The next column is withheld under (b)(6) and (b)(7)(C). Agency systems. unitedstatessecretservice.sharepoint.com, gcc.thor.aesir.office.com, graph.microsoft.com, login.microsoftonline.com. Everything else. Daily Mail, New York Post and Decider hosts, plus ad-exchange and ad-verification hosts such as fastlane.rubiconproject.com, match.adsrvr.org and cdn.doubleverify.com. Format. Host names only, no page paths or titles. One page of the web-activity records the Secret Service released for Ronald L. Rowe Jr., then its deputy director, in response to request 20240110. Rows are timestamped Oct. 4 and Oct. 10, 2023, within the request’s October 2023 window. Yellow highlighting appears on the page as photographed. By the author’s count, the agency mailed the records on paper, about 500 pages. Select the image to enlarge it. Editor’s note: The author filed these requests in a personal capacity: five requests received by the Secret Service on Nov. 3, 2023 (log numbers 20240109 through 20240113), and a request received on April 21, 2025. OctoProbe News reviewed the releases and posts them with two redactions, described under Primary documents. Key Takeaways You can confirm an agency’s SharePoint address with public DNS and Microsoft’s own sign-in metadata. No login, no scanning. You don’t need an email address. A name and title are enough for the agency to search a custodian’s records. Microsoft documents where Teams chats, channel posts and shared files are kept. A request that names those places is harder to answer with “no records.” The D.C. Circuit held in 2021 that two other agencies’ browsing histories were not agency records. The Secret Service processed requests for five top officials’ browser histories and closed all five “Granted/Denied in Part,” according to its FY 2024 FOIA log. An April 2025 request returned a sitemap of roughly 660 internal Secret Service sites and 105 pages of blacked-out card statements. The PDF contains no records for the two document requests. How does the OSINT–FOIA loop work? Records requests fail for boring reasons. Yours names the wrong office. It asks for “all communications” and gets a steep fee estimate. It asks for “SharePoint files” and gets “no records,” because nobody searched SharePoint. Open-source intelligence, the research discipline built on public information, fixes much of that. It can tell you the name of an agency’s Microsoft 365 tenant, which cloud it runs in, which offices have their own sites and who holds which job. A request that carries those facts is harder to misread and harder to dodge. The loop runs the other way, too. Every release is a lead sheet for the next request. Interactive · methodThe OSINT–FOIA loop 1 Map. Find the agency’s Microsoft 365 tenant with public DNS and Microsoft’s sign-in metadata. Example: unitedstatessecretservice-my.sharepoint.com 2 Name. Identify the custodian by name and title from bios, press releases and FOIA logs. Example: Deputy Director Ronald L. Rowe Jr. 3 Request. Ask for the custodian’s web logs, SharePoint and OneDrive documents, and Teams messages. Example: “The last 100 documents edited by the custodian” 4 Mine. Read the release for new site names, hosts, offices and custodians, then map again. Example: “SP 2016 Audit Logs,” p. 116 Each release becomes the starting point for the next round of research. Examples are from this guide’s Secret Service requests. Use the buttons or the arrow keys to step through the loop. Step 1: Identify the agency’s Microsoft 365 tenant and SharePoint hosts Many federal agencies run on Microsoft 365. Every Microsoft 365 customer has a tenant, and the tenant’s original name becomes its SharePoint address. Microsoft spells this out: “When you first sign up for Microsoft 365, you create an onmicrosoft.com domain. Even if you later add a custom domain, all your SharePoint and OneDrive URLs use the original onmicrosoft.com domain.” So don’t guess the address from the agency’s email domain. Confirm it with three public checks. None of them touches the agency’s servers. Check DNS. Look up the candidate name, such as [tenant].sharepoint.com, through a public DNS-over-HTTPS service. A name that resolves exists. NXDOMAIN means no such name. Run a made-up control name too. If it fails and yours resolves, your result means something. Read Microsoft’s public sign-in metadata. Microsoft publishes an OpenID Connect discovery document for every tenant so that apps can sign users in. Ask for it by the agency’s email domain, and it returns the tenant’s ID. Ask again with [tenant].onmicrosoft.com. If the IDs match, the SharePoint name belongs to the agency. A region field reading “GCC” marks Microsoft’s government community cloud. Search passive DNS and certificate logs. Services such as SecurityTrails, owned by Recorded Future since January 2022, keep histories of DNS names. Certificate-transparency logs, searchable at crt.sh, list the certificates issued for an agency’s own domains. Both are better at finding an agency’s websites than its SharePoint, which sits behind Microsoft’s certificates. For the command line Three public lookups. None of them touches the agency’s servers. # 1. Does the SharePoint name exist? (DNS-over-HTTPS; NXDOMAIN means no) curl -s "https://dns.google/resolve?name=unitedstatessecretservice.sharepoint.com&type=A" # 2. Which Microsoft tenant signs in this email domain, and in which cloud? curl -s "https://login.microsoftonline.com/secretservice.gov/v2.0/.well-known/openid-configuration" \ | jq -r .issuer,.tenant_region_sub_scope # 3. Does the tenant's original name map to the same tenant? curl -s "https://login.microsoftonline.com/unitedstatessecretservice.onmicrosoft.com/v2.0/.well-known/openid-configuration" \ | jq -r .issuer If the issuer lines match, the domains share one tenant. A GCC sub-scope marks Microsoft’s government community cloud. Know what each result proves. A name that resolves shows that a Microsoft customer by that name exists. It does not show who the customer is. Anyone can register a tenant with a government-sounding name. The tenant-ID match is what ties a SharePoint name to an agency’s own email domains. A name that fails to resolve is a dead end for now, but it may be a typo, a renamed tenant or a retired host. Check again before you write it into a request. Example The Secret Service tenant The Secret Service’s email domain is secretservice.gov. Its SharePoint is not usss.sharepoint.com. That name does not exist. It is unitedstatessecretservice.sharepoint.com, with personal OneDrive storage at unitedstatessecretservice-my.sharepoint.com. Both Secret Service names resolve. usss.sharepoint.com and a made-up control name return NXDOMAIN. For secretservice.gov, usss.dhs.gov and unitedstatessecretservice.onmicrosoft.com, the tenant ID in Microsoft’s sign-in metadata is the same, and the region field reads “GCC.” Start with the host-finder table. A spreadsheet compiled by Redwing Technologies lists 431 FOIA components, nearly all federal, with their known SharePoint hosts. OctoProbe checked every host in it by DNS on Oct. 20, 2026. Of 334 unique names, 282 resolved and 52 did not. Treat it as a starting list, not an answer. Search your agency, then run the three checks yourself.
