posts.title: DHS Lawyers Wrote 24 Pages on Buying Your Phone’s Location Data. They Withheld Every Page of the Analysis.
posts.description: A 2020 Homeland Security legal opinion weighed whether CBP and ICE could use advertising-ID location data without a warrant. Released under the Freedom of Information Act, it comes back as a cover page and 23 pages stamped “(b)(5).”
keywords: Fourth Amendment Is Not For Sale Act
posts.body: The Paso del Norte port of entry on the U.S.–Mexico border at El Paso, Texas, linked to an example phone ad slot. The app, advertising ID and coordinates shown are fictional. Illustration: OctoProbe News; map © OpenStreetMap contributors; U.S. flag via Wikimedia Commons (public domain). How does the U.S. government use commercial phone advertising data to track location? Federal agencies have bought location data harvested from phone apps and ad auctions, keyed to each phone’s advertising ID, without warrants. DHS lawyers analyzed the legal risks in a 24-page 2020 opinion. A FOIA release shows the department withheld all of its legal reasoning, while oversight bodies found agencies skipped required privacy reviews. On Sept. 25, 2020, the Department of Homeland Security’s top lawyer signed a memo with a plain subject line: “Legal Implications of Advertising Identifier Geolocation Data Use by CBP and ICE.” It went to the department’s chief privacy officer. Its opening paragraph promised a review of “potential challenges under the Fourth Amendment and the Privacy Act of 1974” and of “some proactive measures” the department “may implement to mitigate certain legal risks.” That paragraph is all the public gets. When DHS released the opinion under the Freedom of Information Act, pages 2 through 24 came back blank except for a stamp reading “(b)(5),” the exemption for privileged internal deliberations. Four other legal memos in the same release, on social media monitoring, open-source intelligence and the Privacy Act, got the same treatment. Of 93 pages, 87 were withheld in full. The missing pages matter because the practice is not hypothetical. DHS’s inspector general found that Customs and Border Protection ran more than 55,000 queries of what the department calls “commercial telemetry data” in fiscal 2019 and 2020, and that Immigration and Customs Enforcement ran more than 16,000 in fiscal 2020 alone. The FBI bought its own seat on the same kind of portal in February 2020. The legal reasoning that let these agencies skip a warrant is still secret. This report reads the released pages, the FBI’s contract file and the public oversight record side by side. Interactive explainers show, with made-up data, how an app’s ad slot becomes a location feed and how a buyer turns that feed into a list of phones. All six primary documents are posted unaltered at the end. Editor’s note: The DHS records in this report were obtained through FOIA request 2024-HQFO-00696, filed in January 2024 by the author in a personal capacity. OctoProbe News reviewed the full release and posts it as received. Maps, device records and identifiers in the interactive figures are generated illustrations; no real person, device or location history is depicted. Key Takeaways DHS released one page of its Sept. 25, 2020 legal opinion on advertising-ID location data. The other 23 pages, the legal analysis, were withheld under FOIA exemption (b)(5). Across five DHS legal memos in the same release, 87 of 93 pages were withheld in full. The inspector general counted more than 55,000 CBP queries in fiscal 2019–2020 and more than 16,000 ICE queries in fiscal 2020, and found ICE used the data from September 2018 without an approved privacy assessment. The FBI bought one Venntel Portal seat, with “12,000 queries per year,” through a reseller in February 2020. Why it wanted the data is classified until 2045. Central Command told Congress in April 2026 it had threat reports of adversaries exploiting commercial location data to target U.S. personnel. Read all six primary documents, hosted in full. What did DHS lawyers say about buying phone location data? The opinion was written by Chad R. Mizelle, then the senior official performing the duties of DHS general counsel, for Dena Kozanas, the chief privacy officer. Its first page is marked “ATTORNEY-CLIENT & DELIBERATIVE PROCESS PRIVILEGED.” The released executive summary describes the scope in a single paragraph: “This memorandum analyzes use by U.S. Customs and Border Protection (‘CBP’) and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (‘ICE’) of commercially available geolocation data associated with the advertising identifier (‘AdID’) present on many modern mobile electronic devices. It assesses the potential legal issues associated with using AdID data as a law enforcement tool.” The next sentence says it “reviews potential challenges under the Fourth Amendment and the Privacy Act of 1974.” Then the text stops. A large “(b)(5)” fills the rest of the page, and the next 23 pages, Bates numbers 2024-HQFO-00696-000002 through -000024, carry nothing else (PDF pp. 2–24). The only released page of DHS’s Sept. 25, 2020 opinion on advertising-ID location data. Pages 2–24 were withheld in full. Source: DHS FOIA 2024-HQFO-00696, Bates 000001 (PDF p. 1). The release does not say what the lawyers concluded, which risks they ranked highest, or which “proactive measures” they recommended. It does not show whether anyone acted on the advice. The question the opinion answers was already on the table inside DHS. On June 19, 2019, more than a year earlier, a DHS Privacy Office official wrote to colleagues about a program buying data from the broker Venntel. “The PTA was never approved because we had and continue to have significant concerns with this technology,” the official wrote, referring to a privacy threshold analysis. “Prior to receiving the information, did OGC conduct an analysis under the Carpenter case to ensure that we are able to legally acquire it?” That email surfaced in records the American Civil Liberties Union obtained by lawsuit (ACLU release, PDF p. 100). Another page in the same set says a DHS unit had been “instructed to refrain from using any Venntel data until a legal and Privacy ruling has been determined” (PDF p. 115). Exemption 5 covers “inter-agency or intra-agency memorandums or letters that would not be available by law to a party other than an agency in litigation with the agency.” Since 2016, the FOIA statute also says an agency may withhold information only if it “reasonably foresees that disclosure would harm an interest protected by an exemption,” and it must consider releasing the parts that can be separated out. DHS released one paragraph out of 24 pages. What is ad-tech location data? Every modern iPhone and Android phone carries a resettable string of letters and numbers meant for advertisers. Apple calls its version the Identifier for Advertisers, or IDFA. Google calls Android’s the advertising ID. The industry’s umbrella term is mobile advertising ID, or MAID; the DHS opinion says “AdID.” The ID exists so that ad systems can recognize the same phone across different apps without a name or phone number. That is also what makes it useful to an investigator. An app that shows ads, or that embeds a data-collection kit from a third party, can attach the ID to the phone’s location, the time, the network and a long list of hardware details. A broker that buys enough of those records can draw one phone’s movements over weeks. Agencies insist the data is anonymous. Regulators disagree. In a January 2024 order against the broker X-Mode Social, the Federal Trade Commission said its location data was “not anonymized.” In December 2024 the FTC said Venntel’s parent, Gravy Analytics, collected “more than 17 billion signals from around a billion mobile devices daily” and that the data “can be used to identify consumers and is not anonymized.” After an intruder reached Gravy’s cloud storage in January 2025 and a sample of its data surfaced on a dark-web forum, its parent company, Unacast, described what it licenses: “mostly … mobile advertising IDs (MAIDs), longitude/latitude, and timestamps.” The explorer below shows 56 categories of data that ad exchanges may measure when serving an ad. The list is a wide lens, compiled across multiple exchanges; not every exchange measures every field. Each category is sorted by where it typically comes from: the ad auction’s own bid request, a commercial device database, a data-collection kit inside an app, or a broker’s later enrichment. Some of the most sensitive identifiers on such lists, including the IMEI hardware serial and the SIM card’s ICCID, are not part of the public auction standard at all. They come from apps with deeper device access, or from a lookup that matches a phone model to a catalog. A buyer rarely sees the difference. A delivered record looks like one flat row. Editor’s note: On terms: In intelligence-community usage, “AAID” is shorthand for Apple’s advertising identifier, the IDFA. Elsewhere the same letters often refer to Android: a 2024 CBP privacy assessment writes that Google refers to its identifier as “Google Advertising ID (AAID).” FOIA requesters should spell out which they mean. How does an app turn into a location feed? Location gets into the market two ways. The first is through software development kits, or SDKs: code libraries that app makers bundle for ads, analytics or payments. Some SDKs read the phone’s GPS position directly whenever the app has location permission and send it, with the advertising ID, to the kit’s maker. The Electronic Frontier Foundation reported that the broker X-Mode paid app developers “around 3 cents per user per month” for access to location data. The second is the ad auction itself. When an app has an empty ad slot, it asks an exchange to fill it. The exchange packages a “bid request,” described in the industry’s OpenRTB 2.6 specification, and sends it to many bidders at once, typically within a fraction of a second. The request’s device.ifa field carries the advertising ID “in the clear (i.e., not hashed),” the specification says. A geo object can carry latitude and longitude along with a type code that tells bidders whether the position came from GPS, an IP address lookup, or the user. Every bidder that receives the request sees those fields, including bidders that lose the auction. Nothing in the protocol makes them forget. posts.title: Jailed, Purged, Still Shipping: How ISIS Media Survives the Takedowns
posts.description: A life sentence for its lead narrator and server seizures across Europe and North America have not stopped the Islamic State’s weekly newspaper. Public records show how its online tradecraft adapted: disposable domains, self-hosted chat, a privacy coin, and an archive built never to forget.
posts.body: The masthead of al-Naba, the Islamic State's weekly Arabic newspaper, issue 569 (October 2026), over a map of the Lake Chad region. Logo shown for reporting; illustration and map: OctoProbe Investigations, map © OpenStreetMap contributors. A pro-ISIS chat server has answered at the same web address since March 2019. In that time, Western agencies have purged the movement’s Telegram channels, seized its servers across Europe and North America, and put a central ISIS media figure in a US prison for life. The weekly newspaper still ships every Thursday. That gap — between the force thrown at ISIS media and its stubborn survival — is the subject of this report. It is not a story about one takedown. It is about how the group’s online techniques changed, step by step, as Western collection and enforcement matured against each previous move. Branded channels on mainstream platforms gave way to disposable domains, self-hosted chat, automated bots, a privacy coin, and an archive built never to forget. The techniques below are drawn from public records: domain registration data, DNS, Certificate Transparency logs, court filings, government statements, and published research, organized on the OctoProbe platform. Editor’s note: The Islamic State is a designated Foreign Terrorist Organization. Under OctoProbe’s standards, this report does not name or link any ISIS-run domain, channel, bot, wallet or file; sites are identified by outlet or role only. Key Takeaways A pro-ISIS chat server built on Rocket.Chat software has used one web address since March 2019, outlasting a Europol-Telegram purge and a 2024 server takedown. Five short-lived “feeder” domains went live between October 2022 and March 2023 — three within eight days — and each lasted about three months before vanishing. Court records show the Islamic State ran a central media bureau that leaned on volunteer “supporter networks” to translate and spread its output; a lead narrator for that bureau is serving a life sentence in Virginia. Supporters shifted donations toward Monero, mirror content on the Internet Archive, and migrated chat from Telegram bots toward the encrypted app SimpleX. Public records tie the sites together by name patterns and timing, not by shared infrastructure. Their common use of Cloudflare and privacy proxies is a tactic, not evidence of a single operator. The Central Model, and Why It Still Matters To see what changed, start with what ISIS built at its height. US prosecutors described it in detail in the case of Mohammed Khalifa, a Saudi-born Canadian who was a lead English-language narrator for the group. According to the criminal complaint filed in the Eastern District of Virginia, ISIS “distributed lengthy leadership statements and other violent propaganda through a central media bureau, or the “Diwan of Central Media,”“ operating “primarily through the al-Furqan Foundation for Media Production“ and the al-Hayat Media Center. Khalifa worked inside that bureau from April 2014. The complaint also names the model the group fell back on as its ranks thinned. Because of the volume of content and “military strikes that reduced the ranks of ISIS’s Central Media Bureau, ISIS media leaders such as KHALIFA relied heavily on various supporter networks for propaganda production and dissemination.” Those networks were “groups of individuals who provided support to ISIS but were not necessarily geographically located in Syria or Iraq,” and they handled translation into English and other languages. In his statement of facts, Khalifa agreed that from 2016 he “directed various supporter networks that assisted in the translation, production and dissemination of propaganda released under various ISIS media brands.” Khalifa was charged in 2021 with conspiring to provide material support to ISIS resulting in death. He pleaded guilty to a criminal information and, in July 2022, was sentenced to life in prison (case 1:21-cr-271). The Justice Department said he “served as a lead translator in ISIS’s propaganda production and the English-speaking narrator on multiple violent ISIS videos.” That is the structure the rest of this story watches erode and adapt: an official central bureau, surrounded by a cloud of dispersed volunteers. Enforcement has steadily removed the easy, branded, mainstream-platform ways those two layers used to connect. The techniques that follow are the workarounds. The Server That Never Moved What they did. For years, ISIS distribution ran through mainstream platforms — Twitter, then Telegram above all. What forced the change. When those platforms began removing accounts faster (see the takedown record below), supporters moved part of the operation onto infrastructure they controlled outright. What they do now. The clearest example is TechHaven, a private chat service running Rocket.Chat, free software that lets anyone host a messenger. Bavaria’s domestic-intelligence agency told Bavarian Radio (BR) the platform is run by people “die ideologisch überwiegend dem Islamischen Staat (IS) zuzuordnen sind“ — people who can be assigned predominantly to the Islamic State ideologically. Researchers Alessandro Bolpagni and Ali Fisher, writing through the Italian institute ITSTIME, concluded that “based on the creation date of the first rooms, TechHaven was established around December 2018,” and by March 30, 2026, it had “561 rooms and 12,349 users.” Its current domain was registered in March 2019, according to the registry’s public RDAP record, and security certificates for it appear in public logs from that month through this one. BR reported the chat sits behind Cloudflare; Matthias Rosche of Orange Cyberdefense told the broadcaster that “hinter der URL des Chats “TechHaven” liegen zwei IP-Adressen, die beide Teil des Cloudflare-Netzwerkes sind“ — two IP addresses behind the chat’s address, both part of Cloudflare’s network. Public DNS still shows the same arrangement. The logic is durability. When Europol and Telegram struck in November 2019, BBC Monitoring noted that an administrator of a pro-IS Rocket.Chat service was already warning users away from Telegram. The server, registered eight months earlier, came through untouched. Our evidence and confidence. An OctoProbe investigation seeded with the chat server’s public links resolved its DNS, certificates, and Cloudflare front, and clustered its associated channels and bot around a single subject. Confidence: high that the server exists, has persisted since 2019, and sits behind Cloudflare (named researchers, plus public DNS, RDAP, and CT logs). Its operators are not identified in any public record. Throwaway Domains Behind Cloudflare What they did. ISIS translation and archive hubs once lived at stable addresses. What forced the change. As referral units and monitors learned to flag and report those addresses, long-lived domains became liabilities. What they do now. Operators treat web domains as consumables, cycling through cheap ones on consumer top-level domains and hiding the origin behind a shared content-delivery network. Tech Against Terrorism, a UN-backed initiative, observed the pattern as early as 2022: a translation site for IS content “has changed domains on at least eight occasions since we began our monitoring of it in late 2021,” and prominent ISIS sites “more frequently migrate to a new URL or top-level domain compared to other types of TOWs“ — terrorist-operated websites. Aaron Zelin of the Washington Institute put the tactic plainly in March 2025 congressional testimony: “To make these websites more difficult to take down, IS jumps domain names, often using different country codes to hide in plain sight.“ The records reviewed for this story show the pattern in miniature. Among the links reviewed, a cluster of five short-name “feeder” domains — three on the .blog extension, the others on other consumer top-level domains — first appeared in public certificate logs between October 24, 2022, and March 17, 2023, three of them within eight days that March. None shows a certificate after mid-2023. Because the automatically renewed certificates these sites use last 90 days, each domain likely went dark within about three months of its last certificate. A sixth address, on a country-code domain, now resolves to a domain-parking company. All of them front through Cloudflare, and all list their registrant as a privacy-proxy service through a US registrar. First certificate to latest sign of life, by role, with site names withheld. Bars for deleted domains end when the last 90-day certificate expired, an upper bound. Sources: crt.sh and SSLMate Cert Spotter certificate logs, registry RDAP, and Google Public DNS, queried October 19, 2026. Chart: OctoProbe Investigations. No public seizure notice appears on any of the five. A seized domain usually points to a government banner; these simply stopped resolving, which is equally consistent with a host suspension, a lapsed registration, or operators moving on. The records cannot say which. Our evidence and confidence. Confidence: high on the lifespans, the fronting, and the cadence, all from public CT logs, RDAP, and DNS queried October 19, 2026. Confidence: medium that these specific domains belong to one brand family: they share a name pattern and were co-listed on pro-ISIS index pages, but no public report names these exact hosts. Crucially, the shared use of Cloudflare and of a registrar’s default privacy service proves nothing about who runs them — millions of ordinary sites use the same services. It is a tactic, not a link. Telegram, Bots, and the Move to SimpleX What they did. After 2015, Telegram was the backbone of ISIS distribution. What forced the change. A November 2019 Europol-Telegram action (detailed below) and steady pressure since made channels short-lived. What they do now. Supporters automate the churn and are migrating to encrypted alternatives. Europol said after the 2019 operation that new channels were quickly disabled “despite the use of bots to share join chat links.” That automation has only deepened. The Institute for Strategic Dialogue (ISD) reported in 2026 that official-news channels “are operated by bots and link to a SimpleX channel,” an encrypted messenger that needs no phone number or central directory. ISD added: “Like clockwork, every Thursday, new stand-alone channels are created to distribute the official al-Naba weekly newsletter.“ Our evidence and confidence. An OctoProbe investigation seeded with the chat server’s public links also surfaced live Telegram links — a bot and two channels — clustering around the same subject. Confidence: high on the pattern (automation, disposability, the move toward SimpleX), which is documented by Europol, BBC Monitoring, and ISD. Per OctoProbe’s standards, no channel or bot identifier is reproduced. The Money: A Limited Turn to Monero What they did. Early ISIS crowdfunding leaned on Bitcoin. What forced the change. As blockchain analysis matured, Bitcoin’s public ledger became a liability. What they do now. Some supporter outlets shifted, selectively, to Monero, a cryptocurrency designed to hide senders, receivers, and amounts. Researcher Animesh Roul wrote for the Global Network on Extremism and Technology (GNET) that one pro-ISIS portal “announced the change in the medium of donations from Bitcoin to Monero exclusively in June 2020.” Spain’s Interior Ministry said the translation network ran fundraising campaigns from its own sites, posting “direcciones de criptomonederos como códigos QR“ — wallet addresses as QR codes. The adoption is real but limited, and its results are, by design, unknowable. A Monero address cannot be traced the way a Bitcoin address can, so this report makes no claim about how much, if anything, any ISIS-linked wallet received. Our evidence and confidence. The OctoProbe investigations surfaced Monero wallet strings associated with the link cluster. Confidence: medium. The shift to Monero is well sourced, but on-chain receipts for a privacy coin are not recoverable, and we draw no conclusion from the wallets themselves. Archive.org, and a Policy That Favors Persistence What they did. ISIS content was posted to paste sites and social platforms that increasingly deleted it. What forced the change. Faster takedowns meant links rotted. What they do now. Supporters pair their content with copies on the Internet Archive, whose mission is to preserve, not revise, the record. The behavior was documented years ago. The threat-intelligence firm Flashpoint found in 2018 that Archive.org links were the most common type on two pro-ISIS forums. Analyst Ken Wolf told the BBC that “the use of [the Internet Archive] has allowed the group to achieve persistence whenever content posted to a site such as justpaste.it is removed for violating terms of service,” and that supporters appeared to be “actively archiving pages after creating them.” Later work found the same: ISD’s “Cloud Caliphate” study mapped one of the largest known IS repositories, and a 2023 GNET analysis found “a network of eight mutually interconnected profiles on the Internet Archive“ sharing thousands of productions. Why does it work? Because archiving sites exist to keep things. Tech Against Terrorism’s content-alert data found archiving services removed only 57 percent of the terrorist material flagged to them — the lowest rate of any platform type it measured — leaving, in that sample, “1687 URLs (out of 3936 URLs) remained online at the time of writing.” Its analysts added that this is “perhaps unsurprising given archiving sites have an important mission statement to archive and therefore preserve online content.” The Internet Archive’s own policies describe a library that documents the web rather than polices it. Its mission, the organization says, is “to help preserve those artifacts and create an Internet library for researchers, historians, and scholars,” and more broadly “to provide Universal Access to All Knowledge.” It collects “web pages that are publicly available“ and notes that “some sites are excluded by direct site owner request.” Its Terms of Use say that when authors or publishers ask to be left out, “then we may remove that portion of the Collections without notice,” and that the Archive “may, in appropriate circumstances and at its discretion, remove certain content or disable access to content that appears to infringe the copyright or other intellectual property rights of others.” Removal requests, its help center says, “initiate a review by our team,” with “no guarantees beforehand about the outcome of a request.” The Archive does act against the most violent material when alerted. Its Chris Butler told the BBC that “much of this content is taken down promptly upon our being made aware of it, for example content with executions or personal threats.” The point is not that the Archive endorses this content — it does not — but that a mission to document the internet, combined with reactive, request-based removal, leaves a durable place for backups to sit. Our evidence and confidence. Confidence: high. Every claim here rests on the Internet Archive’s published policies and on multiple independent sources — Flashpoint via the BBC, ISD, GNET, and Tech Against Terrorism. This report does not characterize the Internet Archive’s intent beyond what its own policies and the cited sources say, and it does not link to any archived ISIS material. File Handling: What the Metadata Shows What they did and what changed. The group’s film-studio era produced heavily post-produced videos. Today’s output is leaner — a weekly text-and-infographic newspaper and short, raw attack clips pushed out within days. One narrow, checkable question is what the files themselves carry. OctoProbe examined two ISIS media files supplied for this report: a promotional banner for the weekly newspaper al-Naba, and an Amaq News Agency video of an October attack in Nigeria (both discussed below). posts.title: CEFC, PLA Base 311, and the Long Gap from FBI Surveillance to Designation
posts.description: FBI agents were watching a Confucius Institute in Texas by November 2008; the State Department designated the Confucius Institute U.S. Center in August 2020. In between, CEFC China Energy’s own filings and outside studies tying it to PLA Base 311 were public. CEFC China Energy, Part 1.
posts.body: Cover. A page from FBI FOIA release 1621862-000, dated December 1, 2008. The map pin marks the city of Fuzhou, home of PLA Base 311, not a specific facility. Map © OpenStreetMap contributors. The documents in this analysis support one central finding: it took nearly a decade to go from physical surveillance to designation on the national side. FBI records released under the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) show the bureau’s Dallas field office running a counterintelligence case on the Confucius Institute at the University of Texas at Dallas by August 2008. An agent watched the institute’s first-anniversary celebration on November 8, 2008, and formal surveillance logs followed in November 2009. In June 2009, Dallas sent headquarters a memorandum “for dissemination to DOJ NSD,” the Justice Department’s National Security Division. The State Department designated the Confucius Institute U.S. Center as a foreign mission on August 13, 2020. Measured from the last surveillance log in the release, in September 2010, that took nine years and ten months. Measured from the first documented surveillance, it took nearly twelve years. The first national-level restriction this analysis found, a 2018 ban on Pentagon funding for Chinese-language instruction by Confucius Institutes, came nearly ten years after that first surveillance. During those years a second record grew in public view: CEFC China Energy. Its own 2012 annual report says its chairman, Ye Jianming, was deputy secretary-general of CAIFC, which a U.S. congressional commission’s staff later called a front for the PLA’s former General Political Department. Studies by Project 2049 (2013), Singapore’s RSIS (2015), and France’s IRSEM (2021) tied CEFC’s companies and charity to Base 311, the PLA’s political-warfare base in Fuzhou. And CEFC’s charity listed a Confucius Institute on its own partner page. The FBI files never mention CEFC. The two records are separate. This analysis puts them on one timeline to show how long both existed before national action. How Strong Is Each Piece? This analysis rates each claim by the strength of its sourcing. High confidence: a primary document, checked word for word. Examples: CEFC’s 2012 annual report, CEFC’s archived web pages, federal court records, and the FBI FOIA release. Medium confidence: a reputable secondary source, or one source not yet corroborated. Example: the Project 2049 and IRSEM accounts of the Huaxin Training Center. Low confidence: circumstantial, or a source not located. This piece leaves out low-confidence claims or labels them as such. Claim Main source Confidence FBI Dallas ran a counterintelligence case on a Confucius Institute by August 26, 2008, and conducted physical surveillance from November 8, 2008 FBI FOIA release High In June 2009 the case went to FBI Counterintelligence Division with a memorandum for dissemination to DOJ’s National Security Division FBI FOIA release High Ye Jianming was CAIFC deputy secretary-general, 2003–2005 CEFC International 2012 annual report High CAIFC is a front for the PLA’s former General Political Department USCC staff report (2018) High that the report says so Base 311 (Unit 61716) is the PLA’s political-warfare base in Fuzhou Project 2049; Global Taiwan Institute; IRSEM High A CEFC-linked training center supports Base 311 and sits around the corner from it Project 2049 (2013); IRSEM (2021) Medium CEFC described its charity as “fully sponsored by CEFC China” CEFC website, Wayback capture, June 8, 2017 High CEFC’s charity listed a Confucius Institute and IAGS as partners CEFC NGO website, Wayback capture, April 17, 2017 High CEFC’s charity served as a corporate cover for influence work Assessment based on Project 2049, RSIS, CEFC, and Justice Department records Medium (analytic judgment) The Timeline: From the First FBI File to Designation Entries marked FBI come from FBI FOIPA release 1621862-000 (a 144-page PDF released April 29, 2024). The release concerns the Confucius Institute at the University of Texas at Dallas and does not mention CEFC. All other entries come from separate public sources. Date Record What it shows Source Aug. 26, 2008 FBI Earliest dated record in the release: a Dallas communication on the Confucius Institute at UTD, case pending. PDF p. 14 Nov. 8, 2008 FBI An agent “conducted a physical surveillance of the CONFUCIUS INSTITUTE’s first anniversary celebration” at UTD (record dated Nov. 13, 2008). PDF p. 17 Dec. 1, 2008 FBI The case “was predicated on counterintelligence concerns based on the funding and direction the Institute received from the government of the People’s Republic of China (PRC).” PDF p. 20 June 5, 2009 FBI Dallas notifies FBI Counterintelligence Division and sends a “letterhead memorandum for dissemination to DOJ NSD.” The same record says the Hanban, the institutes’ sponsor, “is an element of the United Front Works Department.” PDF pp. 32–33 Nov. 17, 2009 FBI Agents document people observed at a Confucius Institute directors’ conference in Richardson, Texas (record dated Nov. 24, 2009). PDF p. 41 Nov. 18–19, 2009 FBI First formal surveillance logs: “Physical surveillance of Confucius Institute at University of Texas at Dallas” at a Richardson hotel. PDF pp. 69, 71, 73 July 24–Sept. 17, 2010 FBI Further surveillance logs; the subjects are redacted. PDF pp. 84–105 May 23, 2011 FBI Case closed after “surveillance, extensive asset reporting, interviews, classifies [sic] database searches, and open-source research.” PDF p. 63 2013 CEFC CEFC International’s annual report for 2012 states that Ye Jianming worked “in CAIFC as deputy secretary-general” from 2003 to 2005. Annual report, p. 8 Oct. 14, 2013 Analysis Project 2049 reports that Base 311 is supported by the Huaxin Training Center, tied to a CEFC subsidiary in Fujian. Stokes and Hsiao, p. 29 Dec. 2, 2015 Analysis RSIS lists the China Energy Fund Committee among the civilian and business platforms for which Base 311 served as a military unit cover designator. Raska, CO15262 Summer–Dec. 2015 Allegation A later indictment alleges that the head of CEFC’s charity offered Gal Luft’s think tank $350,000 a year and that the charity sent $350,000 in December 2015. Luft indictment, p. 4 Apr. 17, 2017 CEFC Wayback capture of the CEFC NGO partner page lists 孔子学院 (Confucius Institute) and IAGS. Capture June 8, 2017 CEFC Wayback capture of CEFC’s corporate site links “CEFC NGO” and calls the charity “fully sponsored by CEFC China.” Capture Nov. 18, 2017 Court Patrick Ho, head of CEFC’s charity, is arrested in New York. ICE release Feb. 8, 2018 Court Government files notice that it will use Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act information against Ho. Doc. 45 Aug. 13, 2018 National First national-level restriction found: the defense authorization act bars Pentagon funds for “Chinese language instruction provided by a Confucius Institute.” Pub. L. 115-232, § 1091 Aug. 24, 2018 Analysis USCC staff report calls CAIFC “a front organization for the former General Political Department.” Bowe, p. 9 Nov. 14, 2018 Court Pretrial ruling: Judge Preska admits evidence of Ho’s interest in “transactions in or with Iran, and arms transactions” (uncharged conduct) and bars a defense expert on CEFC’s state ties. Doc. 193, pp. 50, 57 Dec. 2018; Mar. 25, 2019 Court Ho is convicted of FCPA and money-laundering offenses, then sentenced to three years. Justice Dept. Aug. 13, 2020 National State Department designates the Confucius Institute U.S. Center as a foreign mission. The action does not close the center or individual institutes. State Dept. Oct. 2021 Analysis IRSEM, the French Ministry for the Armed Forces’ research institute, places Base 311’s official address in Fuzhou’s Gulou District, “just around the corner” from the Huaxin training center. IRSEM, pp. 90–91 The gap, computed from the documents: First dated record in the release (August 26, 2008) to designation (August 13, 2020): eleven years, eleven months, and eighteen days. First documented physical surveillance (November 8, 2008) to designation: eleven years, nine months, and five days. First formal surveillance log (November 18, 2009) to designation: ten years, eight months, and twenty-six days. Last surveillance log in the release (September 17, 2010) to designation: nine years, ten months, and twenty-seven days. Case closure (May 23, 2011) to designation: nine years, two months, and twenty-one days. First documented surveillance to the first national-level restriction (August 13, 2018): nine years, nine months, and five days. What the FBI Files Show The earliest dated record in the release is an August 26, 2008, communication from FBI Dallas about the institute, which had opened at the university the previous November. By November 2008, agents were in the field. A record dated November 13, 2008, reports that on November 8 the writer “conducted a physical surveillance of the CONFUCIUS INSTITUTE’s first anniversary celebration” at the university. About sixty people attended. The agent noted four unidentified men in suits who “were treated deferentially.” FBI Dallas record dated November 13, 2008, describing physical surveillance on November 8, 2008. Classification markings are struck through as released; the boxes are FBI redactions. FBI FOIPA 1621862-000, PDF p. 17. View the full page. A December 1, 2008, communication states the basis for the case. FBI Dallas communication dated December 1, 2008, stating the case’s predication. Classification markings are struck through as released; the boxes are FBI redactions. FBI FOIPA 1621862-000, PDF p. 20. View the full page. By June 2009 the case had gone to headquarters, with a memo meant for the Justice Department. The synopsis of a record dated June 5, 2009, reads: “To notify Counterintelligence Division of [redacted] and transmit necessary letterhead memorandum for dissemination to DOJ NSD.” FBI Dallas to Counterintelligence Division, June 5, 2009, transmitting a letterhead memorandum “for dissemination to DOJ NSD.” FBI FOIPA 1621862-000, PDF p. 32. View the full page. The same June 2009 record gives the field office’s view of the sponsor: “The Hanban is an element of the United Front Works Department, which is an element of the Chinese Communist Party. This means that the Confucius Institutes are actually under the control of the PRC government.” The passage recurs in later records. It is the Dallas office’s assessment, not a finding by the bureau as a whole. FBI Dallas assessment of the Hanban, as repeated on an undated continuation page. The passage first appears in the June 5, 2009, record (PDF p. 33). FBI FOIPA 1621862-000, PDF p. 46. View the full page. Formal surveillance logs began in November 2009. On November 17, agents observed a Confucius Institute directors’ conference in Richardson, Texas, sponsored by the UTD institute. A log dated the next day records “Physical surveillance of Confucius Institute at University of Texas at Dallas” near a Richardson hotel. Physical-surveillance log, November 18, 2009. FBI FOIPA 1621862-000, PDF p. 69. View the full page. The case closed on May 23, 2011. The closing summary says the “[i]nvestigation to date has benefitted from surveillance, extensive asset reporting, interviews, classifies [sic] database searches, and open-source research.” Closing communication, May 23, 2011. FBI FOIPA 1621862-000, PDF p. 63. View the full page. Two limits apply. CEFC does not appear anywhere in the release, so it says nothing about whether the FBI examined the company. And the release is one field office’s file; it does not show what other agencies held. CEFC’s Chairman and CAIFC A 2018 staff report for the U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission, Alexander Bowe’s China’s Overseas United Front Work: Background and Implications for the United States, says the China Association for International Friendly Contact (CAIFC), “a front organization for the former General Political Department, performs dual roles of intelligence collection and conducting propaganda and perception management campaigns.” The commission notes that the report’s release “does not necessarily imply an endorsement by the Commission.” CEFC International, the company’s Singapore-listed arm, disclosed Ye’s CAIFC post in its own 2012 annual report: “From 2003 to 2005, Mr. Ye Jianming has been working in CAIFC as deputy secretary-general.” That is the strongest single piece of the CEFC record, because it is the company’s own statement to investors. Project 2049 adds a caveat: Ye “was deputy secretary general of CAIFC, or possibly CAIFC’s Shanghai branch, from 2003 to 2005.” Base 311 and CEFC’s Fuzhou Footprint Base 311, also known as Unit 61716, is the PLA’s main base for “three warfares” operations against Taiwan. Writing for the Global Taiwan Institute in 2017, Elsa B. Kania called it the “Public Opinion Warfare, Psychological Warfare, and Legal Warfare Base.” Mark Stokes and Russell Hsiao’s 2013 Project 2049 study, The People’s Liberation Army General Political Department: Political Warfare with Chinese Characteristics, reports that “The 311 Base oversees at least six regiments responsible for psychological warfare and propaganda targeting public opinion on Taiwan” and that “The 311 Base’s commercial persona is the China Huayi Broadcasting Corporation (CHBC).” The CEFC link runs through a training center. Project 2049 reports that “The 311 Base is supported by the Huaxin Training Center (华信培训中心), which is affiliated and collated with a subsidiary of the China Huaxin Energy Company—the Fujian Huaxin Holding Company.” China Huaxin Energy (中国华信能源有限公司) is the Chinese name of CEFC China Energy. The study names Lan Huasheng as general manager of the CEFC Fujian Holding Company and adds: “Lan concurrently serves as CEFC deputy secretary general and executive director of the China Institute of Culture.” It also states that “CEFC has a cooperative relationship with GPD-related organizations, such as the Nishan Forum and the GPD 311 Base.” In those two sentences, “CEFC” means the China Energy Fund Committee, the company’s charity. Location. Project 2049’s footnotes place the training center at 3 Meifeng Road (梅峰路3号) in Fuzhou, “co-located with the 61070 Unit,” which the study identifies as Base 311’s network propaganda center. A 2021 report for IRSEM, the French Ministry for the Armed Forces’ strategic research institute, went further. Paul Charon and Jean-Baptiste Jeangène Vilmer’s Chinese Influence Operations: A Machiavellian Moment says Base 311’s “headquarters are in Fuzhou, the capital city of Fujian, a province that faces Taiwan. Several recent official websites indicated that its address is 77 Meizhu Street, in the city’s Gulou District” (pp. 90–91). The authors found a public pool at that address. From satellite imagery, they identified a site “several dozens of meters to the north that resembles a military site.” They conclude that “the site is just around the corner from the Huaxin training center affiliated to Base 311” (p. 91) and that Unit 61070 “is located a few buildings down from Base 311, at 3 Meifeng Street” (p. 111). IRSEM also says that “The Huaxin Training Center, which is connected to CEFC China Energy, is affiliated to Base 311 as well” (p. 110). It reports that Huaxin Holdings, the Fujian company, “was founded in September 2005—the same year as Base 311—by CEFC China Energy Co. Ltd” (p. 117); CEFC International’s 2012 annual report dates Ye’s founding of Fujian Huaxin Holdings to 2006. Citing the Taiwan-based analyst J. Michael Cole, IRSEM adds that “the CEFC China Energy think tank rented office space in Base 311’s offices” (p. 117). That last point is secondhand and is rated low confidence here. On IRSEM’s account, then, CEFC’s Fuzhou footprint was around the corner from Base 311. posts.title: North Korea’s Fake IT Workers: Thin Covers, Borrowed Lives
posts.description: Most of the eleven Gmail accounts DOJ tied to North Korean IT workers in Operation Lonestar Roundup had thin covers: job-tool sign-ups, empty Google Maps profiles, and new accounts. One rode what looks like a real American’s long online history.
posts.body: Cover. The North Korean national flag over a map of Northeast Asia. No faces or personal data shown. Map © OpenStreetMap contributors. Most of the eleven Gmail accounts that the Justice Department tied to North Korean IT workers in Operation Lonestar Roundup had thin covers: sign-ups to job tools, empty Google Maps profiles, and accounts only months old. One account was different. It sat on top of what looks like a real American's long online history, the kind of borrowed history the FBI warns about. OctoProbe ran every address through public sources between October 19 and 20, 2026. We looked at Google Maps contributor profiles, social and professional networks, freelancer sites, account creation dates, and breach records. Then we checked whether any of the eleven personas shared a phone, a recovery email, or a name. They did not. The cover stories were kept apart from each other. The weak points were inside each persona. Key Findings Thin covers were the norm. Ten of the eleven addresses had at least one public account sign-up. Most were job-hunting tools like Zoom, Calendly, HackerRank, and freelancer sites. One returned nothing at all. (Medium confidence; sign-up checks can misfire.) Empty Google Maps profiles. Eight of the eleven Google accounts have a public Maps contributor page. Only two show any activity. (High confidence for the three pages we captured; medium for the rest.) New accounts. Where we could date an account, most were created in 2025 or 2026. (Medium-high confidence.) One persona reviewed a staffing firm. The "J.Y." persona left a single five-star Google review of Artech, an IT staffing firm in Morristown, New Jersey, about its onboarding process. Artech is not accused of anything. (High confidence the review exists; low confidence on what it means.) One account rode a real person's footprint. The "R.G." account carries years of activity across several platforms under one consistent, real-looking name. (High confidence the footprint exists; low confidence on who controls it.) No cross-links found. No shared phone, recovery email, or name connects any two of the eleven in public data. (Medium-high confidence.) What DOJ Announced, and What It Did Not Say On October 13, 2026, the Justice Department announced charges against fourteen people, two arrests, and the seizure of approximately 187 computer devices. Between September 21 and September 25, the FBI searched more than forty Texas residences known or suspected to be "laptop farms." A laptop farm is a home where a U.S. helper keeps company laptops running so that workers abroad can log in and appear to be in America. A federal grand jury in the Northern District of Ohio returned the indictment. It charges two Americans, Michael James Bostelle and Juan Cecilio Pena Carrillo, and ten China-based defendants. Two more defendants remain under seal. The U.S. Attorney's Office in Ohio said the alleged scheme reached more than seventy U.S. companies. The defendants are presumed innocent unless proven guilty. The Justice Department also wrote that "Investigators discovered that the DPRK operatives allegedly used a network of fraudulent email accounts to facilitate their criminal activity." It then listed eleven Gmail addresses in full in its press release. We mask them here: B***8, M***z, r***g, m***2, a***1, d***g, d***1, y***5, t***n, a***2, and t***8, all at gmail.com. The same addresses appear in a court order from the Northern District of Texas. It orders Google to hand over records on each account. The government's application describes the accounts "as being utilized by DPRK IT workers to fraudulently obtain employment in the United States." The Texas U.S. Attorney's Office announced the Lonestar searches. DOJ does not say which defendants, if any, used these eleven accounts. Nothing in this article ties the Gmail list to Bostelle or Pena. The order also asks Google for "All Google accounts linked to the TARGET ACCOUNTS by cookies; recovery, secondary, forwarding; or alternate email address; Android ID; IMEI; IP address; or telephone number, including SMS recovery number or sign-in account number." In plain terms, investigators want every other account the same people touched. The Texas order asks Google for every account linked to the eleven Gmail addresses. Source: U.S. District Court, N.D. Tex., order, p. 3. How Thin Were the Personas? Thin. The common pattern was a job seeker's starter kit: Zoom, Calendly, HackerRank, Fiverr or Freelancer, the Indian job board Naukri, Replit, Canva, and Grammarly. Those tools are everywhere. Millions of real job seekers use them. So they describe the cover; they do not link one persona to another. One address, M***z, returned nothing on any source we checked. Google Maps told the same story. Eight of the eleven Google accounts expose a public Maps contributor page. Six of those eight are blank. We captured three of the empty pages ourselves, for a***2, t***8, and y***5. Three more read as empty in our lookup data but were not captured. Three of the DOJ-listed Google accounts have public Maps contributor pages with no reviews or photos. Captured October 20, 2026. The accounts we could date were young: A.K. (a***1): A Microsoft profile under an obviously invented name, created January 8, 2026, plus a Freelancer account. A.O. (a***2): A Microsoft account created June 9, 2025, plus HackerRank, Adobe, and Zoom. B***8: A Trello account created April 28, 2025, and last active the same minute. It was made and abandoned. We read that date from Trello's account ID, which embeds its creation time. J.Y. (d***g): A Behance portfolio page created March 23, 2026. The J.Y. persona's Behance page lists "USA" and a member-since date of March 23, 2026. It shows no work. Name and photo redacted by OctoProbe. Captured October 20, 2026. The CrowdStrike report that DOJ linked lists "New public profiles on LinkedIn, Twitter, GitHub, or freelancer platforms" as a warning sign. That fits what we found. The "J.Y." Persona Reviewed a Staffing Firm The J.Y. persona (d***g) had the most consistent cover. The same display name appears on the Google account, a Google Maps Local Guide profile, and Behance. The address is also registered with Calendly, HackerRank, Naukri, and Zoom. Its single Maps review is a five-star review of Artech, an IT staffing firm, at its Morristown, New Jersey, office. Google showed it as "4 months ago" on October 20, 2026, which puts it around June 2026. The excerpt reads: "I'm currently going through the onboarding process with Artech, and I'm already impressed. [three named recruiters] have been incredibly supportive, always responsive, clear in communication, and genuinely helpful at every step." The review names three Artech recruiters. We do not repeat their names. An owner response thanked the reviewer. The J.Y. persona's only Maps review praises onboarding at Artech. Reviewer name, photo, and the names of three Artech staff redacted by OctoProbe. Captured October 20, 2026. Artech is not accused of wrongdoing. Nothing shows the company knew who was behind the account. Staffing firms are a normal route into IT contract work, and that is why a cover persona might use one. The review tells us the persona was used for a real job process in mid-2026. It does not tell us which company, if any, hired the person behind it. We also found a GitHub account and a TikTok account under a similar handle. The GitHub account was created August 1, 2024, holds no code, and follows two university course accounts in New Zealand. The TikTok account dates to 2018. Both look like unrelated people who share a common name. We do not link them to the persona. One Account Rode a Real Person's Footprint The r***g account looks nothing like the others. Under one consistent, real-looking name, which we abbreviate R.G., it carries years of activity. That includes a professional networking profile with hundreds of followers, a Google Maps profile with reviews and edits, and accounts on Etsy and Behance dating to 2020. Its details also appear in a large 2021 data breach. That is exactly the pattern the FBI described in its October 13 public service announcement: "ITWs pay to use, and apply for employment with, facilitators' social media or professional networking accounts which often contain years of legitimate activity history." ITWs is the FBI's shorthand for IT workers. The FBI warns that North Korean IT workers rent accounts with real history. Source: FBI public service announcement, October 13, 2026. We cannot tell whether R.G. is an identity-theft victim, a paid account renter, or someone who has no idea. So we withhold the name, location, and employer. The Ohio indictment also uses the initials "R.G." for one identity used on company laptops. That may be a different person. We do not suggest a match. Where the OPSEC Cracked OPSEC, short for operational security, is the discipline of not leaving traces. The personas mostly failed inside their own walls. Stolen-password logs. The D.T. persona's (d***1) login details appear in a compilation of infostealer logs, data swept from infected computers, and in a 2025 list of stolen logins. We do not publish the password. Mixed geography. The same D.T. address has more than thirty sign-ups since 2021. Its Microsoft profile was created November 20, 2021, with Germany as the country. Its WPS Office account lists Russia. A borrowed handle. D.T.'s Trello account, created June 19, 2021, uses a short word-and-number handle. That handle also exists on more than thirty other sites. Those accounts belong to plainly different people, from a German Envato member since 2017 to a chess account closed in 2018. One reused handle can pull strangers into an investigation. We publish none of those profiles. No cross-persona links. We found no shared phone, recovery email, or name between any two of the eleven. Both phone numbers in our graph trace to R.G.'s breach records, not to another persona. That is worth saying plainly. CrowdStrike reported that "Network infrastructure within laptop farms was found sharing identifiers across multiple concurrent fake personas, a sign of the operation's scale and coordination." That finding concerns network data that only investigators can see. At the public layer, the walls between these eleven personas held. OctoProbe's identifier graph for the eleven addresses, exported with privacy mode on. Captured October 20, 2026. What the Ohio Indictment Alleges About Building Personas The Ohio case is separate from the Texas Gmail list. Its allegations show what a fuller cover looks like. Prosecutors allege that a China-based defendant directed an uncharged Ohio man to create LinkedIn and other professional accounts so fake résumés could attract employers (¶95, p. 19). The indictment lists diplomas from Charter University, an unaccredited online school (¶90, p. 16). It also describes shell companies. Dark Falls LLC came with websites (¶12, p. 5; ¶17, p. 6). B Succeed LLC, a Texas company, was allegedly used for employment checks (¶28, pp. 8–9). Real phones mattered. In one exchange, a co-conspirator wanted the Ohio man's number for verifications "because it was not a VOIP number" (¶106, p. 21). In another, an actor was allegedly hired to sit an in-person job interview (¶120, p. 23). The failures are just as telling. A fingerprint request burned one stolen identity. A China-based defendant allegedly said, "That sucks because we've been using A.S. for over a year." Paragraph 108 of the Ohio indictment. The uncharged co-conspirator's name is masked by OctoProbe. Source: indictment, p. 21. Logins gave the game away too. The indictment alleges that "MFA was accepted approximately 95% of the time from IP 39.152.179.72, which is owned by China Mobile Communications Corporation and resolves to China" (¶134). MFA, or multi-factor authentication, is the second login check, such as a code sent to a phone. Paragraph 134 alleges that most login approvals came from a Chinese mobile address. The uncharged co-conspirator's name is masked by OctoProbe; the black bars over other names are DOJ's. Source: indictment, p. 26. Other alleged slips: a persona Gmail (m***e@gmail.com) was reached from an Akron, Ohio, internet address (¶129, p. 25). Laptops were moved so companies would not catch the scheme through IP tracing (¶110, pp. 21–22). A list of companies was kept so that no address received laptops for several fake employees (¶115, p. 22). When the uncharged Ohio man was told to register a Texas company to open bank accounts, he allegedly replied, "It looks like money laundering." (¶102, p. 20). Scorecard Persona Name seen Maps activity Datable accounts Backstop depth B***8 Trello display name only None surfaced Trello, April 2025 Thin M***z None None None None found R.G. (r***g) Consistent, real-looking Reviews and edits 2020–2022 Deep, likely borrowed m***2 None Empty Google, last seen 2024 Thin A.K. (a***1) Obviously invented None surfaced Microsoft, January 2026 Thin J.Y. (d***g) Consistent on three sites One review Behance, March 2026 Moderate D.T. (d***1) Short handle Empty Microsoft and Trello, 2021 Thin, exposed Y.C. (y***5) One site Empty (captured) None Thin t***n None Empty Google, last seen 2024 Thin A.O. (a***2) One site Empty (captured) Microsoft, June 2025 Thin t***8 None Empty (captured) None Thin The Pattern Is Not New The FBI has warned about these schemes for years, in a 2022 joint advisory, a 2023 U.S.–South Korea notice, and public service announcements in May 2024, January 2025, and July 2025. DOJ announced earlier nationwide actions in June 2025 and November 2025. The newest FBI notice adds a churn warning: "ITWs tend to rotate through bank accounts, street addresses, social media accounts or other identifiers at an unusually high rate due to account bans and other disruptions." Young, thin, single-use accounts are what that looks like from the outside. Method and Limits OctoProbe checked each address against public sources: account sign-up checks, breach-presence records, public profile pages, and page captures, then mapped the results onto an identifier graph. Page captures are dated October 19 and 20, 2026. We read every DOJ and FBI document directly. The Ohio indictment is a scanned PDF, so we checked each quote against the page image. There are limits. Our lookup of the Google accounts themselves did not finish, so the Gmail addresses are undated. Account sign-up checks can return false positives. People-search sources returned nothing on Bostelle or Pena. Common tools like Zoom are not evidence that two accounts are linked. Disclaimer Charges are allegations. Every defendant is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court. Tips about North Korean IT-worker schemes go to the FBI at ic3.gov.

posts.title: The Only Public Map of CENTCOM’s War Orders Is Dated 2022
posts.description: A FOIA-released “Anvil Chart” from 2022 is the only public map of the orders behind CENTCOM’s operations, and most of it is withheld. As the Iran war runs on Article II letters, modernization has to start with the authorities.
posts.body: Cover. The U.S. Central Command emblem, the subject of this commentary, and a B-2 Spirit. Images: U.S. Central Command; U.S. Air Force. Map © OpenStreetMap contributors. America has been trading fire with Iran, on and off, since February 28. The president has sent Congress a stack of war-powers letters. CENTCOM, the command running the fight, has put out a steady stream of press releases. Yet the only public map of the orders behind CENTCOM's operations is a four-page chart dated October 27, 2022, and most of its entries sit next to withheld boxes. That chart came out through a Freedom of Information Act request for CENTCOM's "Authorities Anvil Chart." CENTCOM's reply said it "conducted a thorough good faith search and located four pages." It released those four pages, minus everything covered by exemption (b)(1), which protects classified national-security information. Here is the argument. Bombs, drones, and AI tools get the budget headlines. But the Iran war keeps exposing a slower, quieter weakness: authority. Who can order what, under which document, approved by whom, and how fast. Fix that, or the hardware money buys less speed than Washington thinks. What CENTCOM Released U.S. Central Command's response to a FOIA request for the CENTCOM "Authorities Anvil Chart." The released pages carry the stamp "USCENTCOM FOIA 23-0027." The excerpt does not show the letter's date. Source: records obtained through FOIA. An "anvil chart" is a one-page diagram of how a command's guidance flows. It starts broad at the top and narrows to the orders troops actually carry out. Two terms matter here. An operation order (OPORD) is a commander's directive to subordinate commanders for carrying out an operation. An execute order (EXORD) is the order, issued through the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs at the defense secretary's direction, that puts a presidential decision to start an operation into effect. Both terms come from the Pentagon's joint dictionary and planning doctrine. CENTCOM released two versions of the chart. One is marked for release to Five Eyes partners ("REL"). The other is the U.S.-only "Non-REL" version. At the top of both are the National Security Strategy, the National Defense Strategy, and the Unified Command Plan. Below them sit CENTCOM's campaign plan, its "Theater Campaign Order 2021-2022," and boxes of numbered contingency and functional plans. At the bottom is a row labeled "Current Operations": OPORDs 16, 28, 29, 30, and 32, plus EXORDs labeled Counter Piracy, MCPI, EMIO, CTF, and YUKON JOURNEY. CENTCOM did not define those abbreviations, and this piece does not guess at them. Page 1, "Anvil Chart (REL)," as of October 27, 2022. CENTCOM struck through the SECRET//REL TO USA, FVEY banners and stamped the pages "Approved for Release." Withheld items are marked "(b)(1)1.4a." Bates number USCENTCOM FOIA 23-0027, 001. Source: records obtained through FOIA. Download the released PDF. Page 3, "Anvil Chart (Non-REL)," the U.S.-only version. Its legend says "Unlinked Plans/Ops are on JWICS," the top-secret network. It also lists "Contingency Planning Guidance (TS – Not on portal)." Bates number USCENTCOM FOIA 23-0027, 003. Source: records obtained through FOIA. Pages 2 and 4 are titled "Removed Orders" and "Removed Plans/Documents." Each shows a single entry, OPORD 31, next to a withheld box. Pages 2 and 4, "Removed Orders" (REL) and "Removed Plans/Documents" (Non-REL). Each lists OPORD 31 beside a "(b)(1)1.4a" withholding. Bates numbers USCENTCOM FOIA 23-0027, 002 and 004. Source: records obtained through FOIA. What CENTCOM Withheld, and Why The letter cites 5 U.S.C. § 552(b)(1), which exempts matters "specifically authorized under criteria established by an Executive order to be kept secret in the interest of national defense or foreign policy." The executive order is E.O. 13526. Its section 1.4(a) covers "military plans, weapons systems, or operations." The letter quoted only the first two items: "military plans, weapons systems." That fits with what's blank. Nearly every withheld box sits beside a plan number, a campaign plan, or an order. Those are military plans by definition, and real war plans should stay secret. But look at what the chart shows even with the redactions. The public version is four years old. It names a "Long-Term Middle East Strategy 2020" and a "Theater Campaign Order 2021-2022." Its own legend warns that unlinked plans live "at a higher classification level." And CENTCOM's search for the chart turned up exactly four pages. It's a map of a filing system. Today's war runs on that filing system. The Legal Stack Under the Iran War Start at the top. Every war-powers letter on Iran reviewed for this piece rests on the president's Article II powers, not on a law passed by Congress. After Operation Midnight Hammer, the June 21, 2025, strike on Fordow, Natanz, and Esfahan, President Trump wrote that he "acted pursuant to my constitutional authority as Commander in Chief and Chief Executive." His March 2, 2026, letter on the February 28 strikes said the same. So did the letters on June 9, June 26 and 28, July 7, July 27 in Iraq, and September 1. The statutes don't fill the gap. The 2001 AUMF, Congress's post-9/11 authorization for military force, covers those who "planned, authorized, committed, or aided the terrorist attacks that occurred on September 11, 2001." The 2002 Iraq AUMF is gone. Congress repealed it, along with the 1991 Iraq authorization, in the fiscal 2026 defense bill, signed December 18, 2025. The Congressional Research Service reports that the House has approved three resolutions, and the Senate one, directing removal of U.S. forces from hostilities with Iran. None of the president's letters cites a statute as authority. The War Powers Resolution sets the clock. The president must report "within 48 hours" after introducing forces into hostilities. Within sixty days, he must stop unless Congress authorizes the fight. The administration's May 1 letter declared that "The hostilities that began on February 28, 2026, have terminated." Fighting resumed in June. Next comes Title 10 versus Title 50. Title 10 of the U.S. Code governs the armed forces. Title 50 covers intelligence work, including covert action, where "the role of the United States Government will not be apparent or acknowledged publicly." The Iran strikes are openly acknowledged military operations. That puts them on the Title 10 side. Under 10 U.S.C. § 164, a combatant commander gives "authoritative direction over all aspects of military operations, joint training, and logistics." CENTCOM is that commander's headquarters, and its OPORDs and EXORDs are where Article II decisions turn into missions. Joint doctrine describes the steps in between. JP 5-0, Joint Planning, is "the keystone document for joint planning." JP 3-0, Joint Campaigns and Operations, covers how campaigns are run. Together they lay out the chain from strategy to campaign plan to contingency plan to order. That chain is the anvil. Midnight Hammer also drew on other commands. Gen. Dan Caine, chairman of the Joint Chiefs, said the strike package "was supported by U.S. Strategic Command, U.S. Transportation Command, U.S. Cyber Command, U.S. Space Command." Cyber and information operations have their own joint publications, JP 3-12 and JP 3-13. But the Joint Staff's public doctrine pages now say "A full list of joint doctrine publications may be found on JEL+. (CAC required)." A CAC is the Pentagon's ID card. Even the doctrine has an access problem. A War That Never Quite Ends CENTCOM's ongoing operations make this concrete. The blockade of Iranian ports resumed July 14. By October 10, CENTCOM said, "Four commercial vessels have been disabled and 135 ships have been turned around." On September 1, it "completed a wave of strikes" on air defenses, radars, and mine-laying gear. On July 29, it "completed a heavy wave of strikes against Iran." Meanwhile, the command ended the Operation Inherent Resolve mission in Iraq on September 30. The Congressional Research Service calls the pattern "intermittent U.S. military action." Each round brings another letter, another set of targets, and another round of approvals. When a war runs in pulses, how fast the authorities move matters as much as how fast the aircraft move. Where Authorities Meet Modernization Munitions. The Lead Inspector General's September report, as quoted by CRS, relayed a Pentagon finding that munitions use "has resulted in strategic inventory shortfalls and revealed industrial base bottlenecks for munition resupply." The BBC reported that the watchdog's figures show more than $22 billion spent on munitions from February through June. Interceptors are the sharpest pain point. CRS cites an April think-tank estimate that the U.S. had used "over half of its Patriot and Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) interceptors." The White House rejects the watchdog's assessment. Counter-drone. The Pentagon's counter-drone task force, JIATF-401, said "The $350 million worth of commitments JIATF-401 has made over the last thirty or so days in support of Operation Epic Fury" covered gear already fielded and gear still on the way. An Air University summary of student research on Epic Fury says ad hoc drone defenses were "severely constrained by fragmented interagency authorities and a lack of pre-authorized defensive postures." It recommends "lowering the delegation of engagement authorities." That is the authorities problem in plain terms. Command and control. Joint all-domain command and control (JADC2) is the Pentagon's plan to link sensors and shooters across services. Brig. Gen. Jeffrey Phillips, the Air Force's deputy chief of staff for warfighter communications and cyber systems, said, "We were building that alternate and that contingency on the fly." Early in the war, airmen borrowed the intelligence community's deployable JWICS kits to get connected. That is the same top-secret network the Non-REL chart points to for its unlinked plans. AI-enabled targeting. Adm. Brad Cooper, CENTCOM's commander, said AI tools "can turn processes that used to take hours and sometimes even days into seconds." He added: "Humans will always make final decisions on what to shoot and what not to shoot and when to shoot." That human step is exactly where authorities live. Speeding up the software does nothing for the approval chain. The Barrier Is the Read-On, Not the Hardware Clearance is not the same as access. A planner can hold a Top Secret clearance, carry orders to a combatant command, and still spend the opening weeks of a deployment discovering that none of those facts unlocks the systems where the mission lives. What they need are read-ons—formal access to a classified program—and a seat in a SCIF, a Sensitive Compartmented Information Facility: an accredited room where classified work is allowed to happen. Intelligence Community Directive 705 is blunt: "All SCI must be processed, stored, used, or discussed in an accredited SCIF." At home station, that space and those accesses are often missing. Units with limited SCIF capacity cannot give incoming planners the terminals, accounts, and need-to-know approvals they need to prepare before they leave. The result is a catch-22: planners are told to learn the mission before arriving, but much of the material is available only after arriving. In theater they learn the operation, the execute orders, and the authorities at the Secret, Top Secret, and ACCM levels on the job. ACCM stands for Alternative Compensatory Control Measures—extra need-to-know controls on classified information when standard protections are not enough and Sensitive Compartmented Information or Special Access Program protections are not warranted, per DoD Manual 5200.01 guidance summarized by the Center for Development of Security Excellence. That is the Anvil Chart problem from the other end. The map exists. CENTCOM's FOIA reply described it as an Authorities Anvil Chart on the command's SIPR portal. But the people who need to click the links get the access late—or never get a working link at all. Legacy portals break. Repositories move. A clearance does not equal an account on the right system, and an account does not equal a completed read-on. The infrastructure backlog makes that worse. A June 2026 Department of War review of the defense research enterprise found that "The Sensitive Compartmented Information Facility (SCIF) accreditation lifecycle is severely extended by manual, sequential reviews," compounded by "a critical shortage" of TEMPEST technical authorities and accrediting officials. GAO told Congress in February 2026 that agencies took an average of 206 days to finish the fastest 90 percent of initial Top Secret clearances—92 days past the 114-day goal—and that average times have trended longer since fiscal 2022. Clearance delays and SCIF shortages are not planner anecdotes. They are audited, public facts. The Fix Not everything here is classified, and fixing it doesn't require breaking secrecy. First, Congress should do its job. With the 2002 AUMF repealed and the 2001 AUMF written for al-Qaeda, the Iran fight rests on Article II and a pile of 48-hour letters. Congress can authorize the war, condition it, or end it. Leaving it to the letters isn't a policy. Second, the Pentagon should treat its authorities map as a weapons system. Give it a single system of record. Put dates on every version. Make sure the links actually work. Let a planner check access before deployment instead of after. When someone clicks on the map, the road should actually go somewhere. Third, push engagement authority down where the threat moves fastest. Drones and missiles don't wait for a slide deck. The Air University research says as much. Pre-delegated, pre-approved defensive authorities cost nothing in munitions, and they don't run out. And fourth, release more. A four-year-old org chart with numbers blacked out tells the public nothing about the actual plans. That's fine. But it also shows the system has room for routine, dated, unclassified authority summaries. Those would cost the enemy nothing and would help the voters paying for the war. Fifth, start the read-ons and the SCIF capacity before the plane leaves. Pre-deployment program access and home-station SCIF seats for planners cost less than lost weeks of on-the-job learning in theater. The implementation standard is the same as for the map: access has to arrive early enough to matter. Peace through strength needs paperwork that works. Records referenced: CENTCOM FOIA response and released pages stamped "USCENTCOM FOIA 23-0027," records obtained through FOIA. The released PDF is available here.

posts.title: Your Taxes, Their Target List: Following NED Money Into Ukraine’s Online Info-Ops Web
posts.description: A $100,000 NED grant went to Prometheus in 2016 for investigations published on InformNapalm, not to Myrotvorets. InformNapalm shares mail servers with Myrotvorets, a digital target list that names Americans and runs “psyops” code.
posts.body: In 2016 the National Endowment for Democracy (NED), which Congress funds, paid $100,000 to the Kyiv nonprofit Prometheus for investigations published on InformNapalm. InformNapalm shares a private mail server with Myrotvorets, a Ukrainian “enemies” database that lists Americans, and has mentioned it in 124 English-language posts since 2015, often citing or promoting it. No record shows NED money reached Myrotvorets. U.S. taxpayer money, Ukrainian officials and a public “enemies” database that lists Americans sit closer together than either government admits. The people overlap, too. Prometheus’ president moved into the government’s own strategic-communications centre. A soldier’s public LinkedIn profile shows service in a military psychological-operations unit while he volunteered for InformNapalm. And Myrotvorets was announced and defended by Anton Gerashchenko, an adviser to the interior minister, whose ministry’s officers attended its 2014 working meeting with InformNapalm. The findings rest on public records: an NED grant list, State Department documents released under the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA), archived web pages, internet domain records and Myrotvorets’ own code. They are narrower than the internet rumors. They are also harder to dismiss. Key Takeaways NED, which Congress funds, gave $100,000 in 2016 to Prometheus for investigations posted on informnapalm.org, though InformNapalm later wrote that it had “not applied for grants.” InformNapalm, the site NED’s grant paid Prometheus to publish on, mentions Myrotvorets in 124 English-language posts from 2015 to 2024 and has repeatedly cited, republished and promoted it. A public LinkedIn profile lists service in a Ukrainian Special Operations Forces PSYOP unit from 2015 to 2016, overlapping with volunteer work at InformNapalm. Prometheus’ former president, once on InformNapalm’s editorial team, became deputy head of Ukraine’s state Centre for Strategic Communication. Interior Ministry adviser Anton Gerashchenko announced Myrotvorets in 2014, called it a card index for special services, and asked prosecutors to drop a case against it; SBU and Interior Ministry officers attended its 2014 meeting with InformNapalm. Archived entries show Myrotvorets listed U.S. citizens, including Tulsi Gabbard, Scott Ritter and Gonzalo Lira, who later died in Ukrainian custody. NED was created in 1983 to do openly what the CIA once funded in secret, its own founders said; no record shows CIA money in NED, Prometheus, InformNapalm or Myrotvorets today. Myrotvorets and InformNapalm route email through the same privately run mail server, linked by public records to one Ukrainian developer. Myrotvorets ships a script named psyops.js that shows visitors a message chosen by their internet address, and its code logs who searches its database. Cover. A snippet of Myrotvorets’ psyops script over a map of Kyiv. Map © OpenStreetMap contributors. What Is Myrotvorets? The Ukrainian “Enemies” Database Explained Myrotvorets means “peacemaker.” It launched in 2014 under the domain psb4ukr.org and now runs at myrotvorets.center. Its main product is a searchable database it calls “Purgatory.” Each entry carries a name, photos, an accusation, and links. Many carry far more. The site describes itself in English in its own header. The archived homepage from September 2, 2026 reads: “Information for law enforcement authorities and special services about pro-Russian terrorists, separatists, mercenaries, war criminals, and murderers” Directly below that line, the same header lists three locations. One of them is “Langley, VA, USA.” Langley is the Virginia community that houses CIA headquarters. We return to that line below. The Myrotvorets homepage as archived on September 2, 2026. The address block at top right lists “Langley, VA, USA.” Source: Wayback Machine. Myrotvorets says it is independent and unfunded by any government. Its donation page, archived November 1, 2021, states in Ukrainian: “Центр не фінансується жодною державною чи недержавною організацією, не належить до будь-якої урядової структури.” In English: the center is not financed by any state or nonstate organization and does not belong to any government structure. Critics call the database a “kill list.” Fact-checkers have pushed back on that label. Newsweek wrote in 2022: “Mirotvorets does not advocate violence against those on its database, and there is no conclusive evidence that it's ever been used as a "kill list," as Waters claims.” Human rights monitors take the doxing seriously. Doxing means publishing private personal details, such as a home address, to expose someone. The Atlantic Council’s Digital Forensic Research Lab (DFRLab) reported in 2017 that the United Nations human rights office had urged Kyiv to act. DFRLab wrote that “Ukrainian authorities were urged to promptly and effectively conduct an investigation to address alleged violations and remove personal data from Myrotvorets.” DFRLab also reported that Ukraine’s own president objected. It wrote: “In June 2016, Ukrainian President Petro Poroshenko condemned Myrotvorets for publishing personal data of more than 4,000 journalists” The U.S. government has weighed in, too. The State Department’s 2023 human rights report on Ukraine says: “The Myrotvorets website, which reportedly maintained close ties to the security services, hosted a database of personal information of journalists and public figures whose statements and activities had been deemed unpatriotic.” Note the word “reportedly.” Washington has never formally tied Myrotvorets to a Ukrainian agency. Neither has Kyiv. Who Runs It The site’s operators stay anonymous. Press reports have long named two men. One is a director using the name Roman Zaitsev. The other is Anton Gerashchenko, a former member of parliament and adviser to Ukraine’s interior minister. DFRLab, citing Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty (RFE/RL), wrote that Zaitsev was a former department head at the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU), the country’s domestic intelligence agency. Asked whether Myrotvorets was his project, DFRLab reported, “Gerashchenko winked, chuckled, and replied: ‘No.’” The Russian-language independent outlet Meduza summarized the record in 2024.
