It wrote that, according to The Times of London, “The Myrotvorets database was created in 2014 by Ukrainian politician Heorhiy Tuka and a former State Security Service (SBU) officer using the pseudonym Roman Zaitsev” The same Meduza piece states plainly: “Myrotvorets is not officially affiliated with the Ukrainian government.” It adds that Zaitsev “has maintained that the website is not controlled by the agency and does not receive state funding.” That is the official story. The records tell a more complicated one. How Close Is Myrotvorets to Kyiv’s Government? Officials, Embassies and the NGO Web Myrotvorets and InformNapalm call themselves volunteers. Ukraine’s diplomats call Myrotvorets a private group. The public record shows something messier: officials in the room and a nonprofit leader who moved into the government’s own messaging shop. An OctoProbe investigation graph maps those ties. It holds 304 nodes, or data points, and 500 links among them, built from 100 queries over 15 rounds of automated lookups. The method behind such graphs is documented separately. A graph analyst seeded it with eight subjects. They included the 2016 NED grantee Prometheus, its co-founder, InformNapalm, a former interior minister and Anton Gerashchenko, a former adviser to the interior minister. Each tie was then checked against public records. Where the graph and the public record agree, we call the link proven. A note on terms. In this section, “embassies” means Ukraine’s own embassies and its Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MFA), whose domain is mfa.gov.ua. The investigation graph contains no British embassy, U.K. government domain, or British official. It contains no embassy domain at all. Every embassy tie below comes from public records. Proven: From Prometheus President to the Government’s Strategic Communications Centre Mykola Balaban is the clearest bridge between the NGO network and the Ukrainian state. He did not hide it. In 2015, Balaban spoke for InformNapalm. At an August 2015 briefing in Kyiv, the Ukraine Crisis Media Center identified him as “a member of InformNapalm portal’s editorial team” It then reported: “According to Balaban, the portal actively cooperates with the law enforcement agencies and Ukraine’s Security Service.” The same report added a diplomatic angle: “The Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine also intends to use these materials during public debates in the United Nations as evidence of the Russian aggression” A 2015 Ukraine Crisis Media Center report on InformNapalm’s cooperation with the SBU and Ukraine’s foreign ministry. Source: uacrisis.org, captured October 16, 2026. By 2017, Balaban was president of Prometheus. InformNapalm’s own write-up of the “Donbas in Flames” launch named “Mykola Balaban, the President of the Prometheus center” That is the same Prometheus that NED paid $100,000 in 2016 for investigations posted on informnapalm.org. The guide itself was funded by Canada’s local-initiatives fund, the same article says. Then he moved inside the government. His official biography for the 2025 Kyiv StratCom Forum reads: “He was the co-founder and the president of NGO Prometheus Centre for Studies of Security Environment; later, he headed the situation centre of the Communications and Public Diplomacy Department of the MFA of Ukraine as an adviser.” The same page lists his current title: “Deputy Head of the Centre for Strategic Communication SPRAVDI” The Centre for Strategic Communication and Information Security, which publishes as SPRAVDI, is part of Ukraine’s state. It runs on a government domain, spravdi.gov.ua. Its mail record points to mail.mkip.gov.ua, the mail server of Ukraine’s Ministry of Culture and Information Policy. The Centre’s own About page says: “The Centre was established as one of the mechanisms for countering disinformation by joint efforts of the state and civil society.” The Centre for Strategic Communication describes itself as a joint project of “the state and civil society.” Source: spravdi.gov.ua, captured October 16, 2026. The investigation graph shows the same arc in data. The Balaban subject node links to a work email on the spravdi.gov.ua government domain and to the Centre’s website. That address is not published here. In short, one person went from InformNapalm’s editorial team, to president of a NED-funded nonprofit, to an adviser in Ukraine’s foreign ministry, to deputy head of a state communications centre. Each step is documented by the organizations themselves. There is nothing illegal about any of it. But it undercuts the picture of fully independent volunteers. The embassy link runs through that Centre, too. A LinkedIn post by the Centre says it presented its work on countering disinformation during a meeting of the heads of Ukraine’s foreign diplomatic missions in 2026. The full post could not be viewed without signing in, so the detail is treated as reported. On LinkedIn: A PSYOP Soldier Who Volunteered for InformNapalm The clearest overlap between Ukraine’s military information units and the volunteer network sits on a public LinkedIn profile. Lukyan Turetsky’s profile lists service as a soldier in the Armed Forces of Ukraine from May 2015 to July 2016. It gives his corps as Special Operations Forces and his unit as “Information and psychological operations (PSYOP).” The same profile lists him as a volunteer at InformNapalm from January 2015 to January 2017. It also lists the 9th company of Maidan Self-Defense in 2013–14. By his own account, then, he served in a military PSYOP unit while volunteering for InformNapalm, for more than a year. The profile does not say what he did for either, or that the roles were connected. A self-reported LinkedIn profile showing overlapping service in a Ukrainian PSYOP unit and volunteering with InformNapalm, 2015–2016. Source: LinkedIn. Other overlaps run through state communications bodies. In 2015, Ukraine’s new Ministry of Information Policy announced cooperation with InformNapalm, Detector Media reported. The Ministry of Information Policy announces cooperation with InformNapalm, March 2015. Source: detector.media. The state Centre for Strategic Communication draws on the same circle. The culture ministry announced in 2021 that Liubov Tsybulska, formerly of the Ukraine Crisis Media Center, would head it. When she left that September, the Institute of Mass Information reported that Balaban, the former Prometheus president, was her deputy. The culture ministry names Liubov Tsybulska to head the state Centre. Source: mincult.gov.ua. IMI reports Tsybulska’s exit and Balaban’s role as deputy head, 2021. Source: imi.org.ua. Balaban still speaks for the Centre abroad. A SPRAVDI release quotes him as its deputy head presenting a handbook to help Ukraine’s diplomats counter disinformation. Balaban’s path from NGO to state, as each organization describes it. Sources: UCMC, Kyiv StratCom Forum, IMI. Government Domains Sit Apart The state’s own websites run separately. Ukraine’s foreign ministry uses its own mail service, run by the security company Proofpoint. SPRAVDI uses the culture ministry’s mail. No shared infrastructure turned up between any .gov.ua domain and the NGO network; the ties to the state run through people and meetings. Proven: Myrotvorets Met InformNapalm With SBU and Interior Ministry Staff Myrotvorets has said it is no part of the state. Its own archive says state officers sat at its table from the start. On December 21, 2014, psb4ukr.org posted a short notice titled, in Russian, “A working meeting of Myrotvorets Center specialists with representatives of the information resources INFORMNAPALM and LOSTIVAN was held.” The archived post says: “На встрече, которая проходила 21 декабря 2014 года, присутствовали также сотрудники оперативных подразделений Центральных Аппратов СБ Украины и МВД Украины.” In English: present at the meeting were also officers of the operational units of the central offices of the SBU and Ukraine’s Ministry of Internal Affairs. The translation is ours. The notice adds that participants discussed “пути взаимного обмена критической информацией”, or “ways of mutual exchange of critical information,” and cooperation with law enforcement and special services of European countries. Myrotvorets’ own notice of a December 21, 2014, meeting with InformNapalm attended by SBU and Interior Ministry officers. Source: Wayback Machine. At the time, Arsen Avakov ran the Interior Ministry. His adviser was Anton Gerashchenko, whom press reports name as a Myrotvorets co-founder. Lawfare wrote in 2023 that Myrotvorets “was co-founded in 2014 by Anton Gerashchenko, then a member of the Ukrainian Parliament and now adviser to the Ministry of the Interior.” The graph includes Avakov’s public social accounts but found no technical link between them and the NGO domains. His tie is through his ministry and his adviser, not through infrastructure. Lawfare also located a 2015 interview. It quotes Zaitsev telling the Ukrainian outlet Fakty: “I repeat, we are not abstract: we work with the state, and the state cooperates with us.” Lawfare on Myrotvorets’ founders and Zaitsev’s 2015 claim of state cooperation. Source: lawfaremedia.org, captured October 16, 2026. Lawfare described a wider ring around both groups. A hacker team called Kyber Sprotyv says it works with InformNapalm and Myrotvorets. Lawfare wrote that “The group’s active cooperation with Myrotvorets, InformNapalm, and the National Resistance Center is beyond any doubt.” The National Resistance Center is a unit of Ukraine’s armed forces. Anton Gerashchenko: The Official Behind Myrotvorets No official is tied to Myrotvorets more closely than Anton Gerashchenko. He announced the site, defended it

posts.title: 25 Pages of Press Clips: Leak Shows How Thin White House Vetting Really Was
posts.description: Leaked 2016 transition files show the White House screened top appointees with newspaper clippings. A 25-page Giuliani research file shows how thin it was, and what a real background investigation covers.
posts.body: Cover. Page one of the leaked Giuliani research file over a map of Washington. Map © OpenStreetMap contributors. The White House vetted its 2016 appointees with newspaper clippings. Leaked transition files prove it. And the federal system meant to dig deeper rewards speed and contracts over depth. The Presidential Personnel Office (PPO), the White House shop that recruits and screens political appointees, controls more than four thousand jobs. Its 2016 files are public. They show a process built for speed, not depth. Take Rudy Giuliani. His business-ties research file runs twenty-five pages. Nearly every line is a quote from a news story. The Leak Distributed Denial of Secrets (DDoSecrets), a nonprofit that archives leaked data, posted the set. It describes the files as “Dozens of documents from the Trump administration transition, including backgrounds and opposition research on potential Trump appointees.” Axios first reported on the documents in 2019. It wrote that “Trump's frazzled transition team foisted the job of political vetting onto the Republican National Committee.” The Republican National Committee (RNC) is the party’s campaign arm, not a background-check agency. Axios reported: “The RNC's team of about two dozen researchers, almost all of whom were in their 20s, faced trying circumstances.” Glaring Issue One: Little Vetting at All One vetter told Axios: “Totally inadequate resources for the overall process. ... We would probably run through dozens [of contenders] a day.” Dozens a day leaves minutes per candidate. And Axios found nothing behind it: “Nobody we spoke to who worked at the senior levels of the transition could point us to any additional political vetting that was done before Trump announced his nominees.” The cost showed up fast. Labor pick Andrew Puzder withdrew after an old domestic-abuse allegation, which his ex-wife later retracted, resurfaced. Axios wrote: “The RNC vetters overlooked a local news report on her allegations.” The RNC pushed back. Spokesman Mike Reed said: “Individuals selected for high-level administration jobs would have gone through more thorough background checks by lawyers, law enforcement agencies, and ethics officials before formally assuming their role.” Glaring Issue Two: Clippings, Not Investigations The leak’s index holds forty-four backgrounders. OctoProbe downloaded every one and counted pages. The median file runs thirteen pages. The shortest runs four. The longest runs forty. The average is about fifteen. The Giuliani business-ties research file is twenty-five pages and 240 kilobytes. Its fifty-five citations point almost entirely to press coverage: The New York Times, the Associated Press, The Wall Street Journal, Bloomberg, Forbes, and Politico, among others. Page one of the Giuliani research file. Each entry quotes a news story. Source: DDoSecrets. The RNC itself called the files “initial pre-interview briefings put together to inform the transition team of top-line issues of note in the candidates' background.” That’s the point. A top-line brief is where vetting should start, not end. Missing from the file: asset searches, court dockets and litigation history, property and corporate records, police reports obtained through the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA), breach data, and open-source intelligence (OSINT), meaning research from public data such as social accounts, registries, and archives. A man with Giuliani’s decades of foreign clients, law firms, and consulting deals would fill hundreds or thousands of pages under that kind of review. The process needs modernizing. Read the full file below. Rudy Giuliani business-ties research file, 25 pages, 240 KB. Download the PDF or view the DDoSecrets original. Glaring Issue Three: Vetters Without Credentials The office doing the vetting was thin, too. The Washington Post reported in 2018: “From the start, the office struggled to keep pace with its enormous responsibilities, with only about 30 employees on hand, less than a third of the staffing in prior administrations, The Post found.” It added: “Since the inauguration, most of the staffers in the PPO have been in their 20s, some with little professional experience apart from their work on Trump’s campaign, The Post found.” The problem carried into 2025. The New York Post reported that PPO director Sergio Gor “has yet to submit official paperwork about his own background needed for a permanent security clearance, according to multiple sources.” The paper said Gor vetted staff “by poring over old tweets, political donations and remarks to ensure loyalty to the president.” It added: “He currently has an interim security clearance, as do some other Trump officials who are awaiting the completion of background checks.” The White House disputed the story. Counsel David Warrington said: “His security clearance is active, any insinuation he doesn’t maintain a clearance is false.” Sources familiar with the office said core PPO staff did not hold security clearances and had no investigative training. The people screening appointees had never been screened that way themselves. Glaring Issue Four: Who Vets the Cleared? Many appointees arrive with federal careers, some of them in classified work. The scope that normally covers that kind of access is far deeper than a stack of clippings. A security clearance is government permission to see classified information. Top Secret access, including Sensitive Compartmented Information (SCI), intelligence held in tightly controlled compartments, requires a Tier 5 background investigation, the top level of federal screening. Tier 5 replaced the Single Scope Background Investigation (SSBI) in fiscal year 2017, according to the Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency (DCSA), the Pentagon agency that runs most federal background checks. It starts with the Standard Form 86 (SF 86), a long questionnaire on residences, foreign contacts, finances, and drug use, per the DCSA case-type table. The FBI laid out what deep screening looks like in its own 2016 transition briefing book, released through FOIA on the FBI Vault. Three pages chart the bureau’s investigation levels side by side. The deepest, Level I, covers the “Entire adult life” and calls for “20-30 interviews.” Every level checks credit, police records in each place a candidate lived, licensing boards, relatives, and time abroad. Types of FBI investigations, Levels I through IV. Source: FBI 2016 Presidential Transition briefing book, page 18, via the FBI Vault. The table continued: interviews, relatives, foreign activity, and records checks. Source: FBI briefing book, page 19. The old Single Scope Background Investigation beside Tier 5, the current standard for Top Secret and SCI access. Source: FBI briefing book, page 20. Tier 5 itself carries a “Seven year scope.” Investigators interview a neighbor, check two employment references, and review divorce records. None of that appears in a clipping file. In January 2025, the president ordered that a list of White House staff be “hereby immediately granted interim Top Secret/Sensitive Compartmented Information (TS/SCI) security clearances for a period not to exceed six months”. That order put access before the investigation. If the investigation trails the access, who checks the people who already handled secrets? The Contract Problem Background checks are big business. The record shows the government keeps paying for volume and speed. In January 2018 the Government Accountability Office (GAO), the investigative arm of Congress, put the clearance system on its High Risk List. GAO said “executive branch agencies are unable to investigate and process personnel security clearances in a timely manner, contributing to a significant backlog of background investigations, totaling more than 700,000 cases as of September 2017.” It also found that “government-wide measures for the quality of background investigations have not yet been established”. Speed was measured. Quality was not. DCSA inherited the backlog. Federal News Network reported in 2025 that the agency cut its caseload “from a peak of 290,000 cases last September to 222,000 in May.” Even then, “the average end-to-end processing time for background investigations is 243 days”. Contractors have gamed the system before. The Justice Department alleged that U.S. Investigations Services (USIS), which did background checks for the Office of Personnel Management (OPM), “deliberately circumvented contractually required quality reviews of completed background investigations in order to increase the company’s revenues and profits.” The practice, the government said, involved “releasing cases to OPM and representing them as complete when, in fact, not all the reports of investigations comprising those cases had received a contractually-required quality review.” USIS and its parent agreed in 2015 to forgo at least $30 million. The Justice Department noted that “The claims resolved by the settlement agreement are allegations only and there has been no determination of liability.” A top Justice official put it bluntly: “Shortcuts taken by any company that we have entrusted to conduct background investigations of future and current federal employees are unacceptable,” said Benjamin C. Mizer. Political vetting runs on a separate track, and it is even looser. In 2016 it was handed to a party committee, the RNC, with “about two dozen researchers”. Transitions lean on allies and their networks, friends of friends, not on firms chosen for investigative depth. OctoProbe’s analysis: both tracks reward the same thing. Contracts and slots go to whoever moves cases fastest or knows the right people. Nobody wins business by turning in the deepest file. What Real Vetting Pulls Twenty-five pages of clips cannot cover a career that spans decades. A real review pulls primary records, the documents themselves rather than stories about them. Federal court filings. PACER (Public Access to Court Electronic Records) holds federal lawsuits, bankruptcies, and criminal cases. State court dockets. Most lawsuits, divorces, and liens are filed in state courts, not federal ones. Securities and money. EDGAR, the Securities and Exchange Commission’s filing database, shows board seats and stock deals. OGE Form 278, the public financial disclosure senior officials file with the Office of Government Ethics, lists assets, income, and debts. Corporate structures. State business registries and beneficial-ownership records show who really owns a company. Sworn testimony. Affidavits and depositions in old lawsuits capture what a person said under oath. Property and liens. County deed and lien records show holdings, debts, and unpaid taxes. Police reports. FOIA and state open-records requests can pull incident reports that never made the news. How deep real vetting goes. The 2016 backgrounders covered only the top layer. Graphic: OctoProbe. Breach Data and the Blackmail Risk The deepest layer is breach data, records stolen from websites and dumped online. It shows the reputational risks no clippings file will ever catch. When the cheating site Ashley Madison was hacked in 2015, FedScoop reported: “More than 15,000 government and military email domains are among the 36 million email addresses released Tuesday night as part of the massive data breach associated with the online infidelity site.” It cautioned: “Not every address is necessarily tied to an actual government employee.” Security reporter Brian Krebs wrote: “The leaked AshleyMadison data could also be useful for extorting U.S. military personnel and potentially stealing U.S. government secrets, experts fear.” Cheating sites are one category. Adult sites and gambling sites are others. Adversaries mine these dumps for leverage. A vetting team that never looks will learn about the problem from a foreign service, or from a blackmailer. This post makes no claim that Rudy Giuliani or anyone else named here held an account on any such site. What Modern Tooling Captures OctoProbe pointed its crawler at the leak itself. In one round it ran 136 queries and built a graph of fifty-one nodes and fifty links. Forty of those nodes are the leaked PDF backgrounders. Each document is stored as an archived copy with MD5 and SHA-256 hashes, digital fingerprints that prove a file hasn’t changed since capture. Every node also links to its live page, its Wayback Machine snapshots, and its latest Archive.ph copy. If a file is altered or pulled, the record survives. OctoProbe graph of the Trump Transition leak, with the David Petraeus backgrounder selected. Click to zoom. That is the floor, not the ceiling. A tool that fingerprints and archives forty files on its own can just as easily pull dockets, deeds, and corporate filings. The 2016 vetters worked from clippings. Bottom Line The 2016 vetting files were short, fast, and built from news stories. The office running them was small and young. Nine years later, its director was reported to be working on an interim clearance. The deeper system is no cure. GAO flagged it as high risk, its backlog has topped 290,000 cases, and one contractor was accused of faking quality reviews to boost profits. Real vetting means dockets, deeds, filings, and breach data. Until contracts reward depth, appointees will keep getting clippings. Disclaimer This analysis relies on leaked documents published by DDoSecrets and on public reporting. It alleges no wrongdoing by anyone named.

posts.title: Alleged Saudi Spy List Leaked by Houthi-Tied Group, and Their Phones Do the Rest
posts.description: A hacker group allegedly tied to the Houthis dumped what it calls a roster of Saudi intelligence officers and stations. The files may be doctored, but the phone numbers in them lead to homes, cars, and app accounts in minutes.
posts.body: Cover. Abstract identifier graph over a map of Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. No faces or personal data shown. Map © OpenStreetMap contributors. A hacker group allegedly tied to Yemen’s Houthi rebels has dumped what it says is a roster of Saudi intelligence officers and their stations around the world. It posted the files on its own website and Telegram channel first. The files list names, ranks, and personal phone numbers. They also list the foreign liaison officers, local collaborators, and drivers who work with Saudi intelligence abroad. This was no whistleblower. It was an enemy trying to burn a rival spy service, and the files may be doctored. But the phone numbers work like keys. OctoProbe used them to reach homes, cars, and app accounts in minutes. The Dump The group calls itself Uways Qarani. It published the dump on its own website on October 4, 2026, and pushed it out on its Telegram channel the same day. The site post carries a taunt: “على جهاز الاستخبارات السعودي أن يعلم أن زمن اللعب في الظلال قد انتهى.” (OctoProbe translation: “The Saudi intelligence service should know that the era of playing in the shadows is over.”) On October 5, a Telegram post billed it as the full database and warned: “نحذّر السلطات السعودية: لقد انتهى عهد التواري في الظل والأمن الوهمي.” (OctoProbe translation: “We warn the Saudi authorities: the era of hiding in the shadows and of false security is over.”) Distributed Denial of Secrets (DDoSecrets), a nonprofit that archives leaked data, republished the material on October 14, ten days later. It called the set “An organizational chart and identity documents identifying hundreds of members of the General Intelligence Presidency (GIP), Saudi Arabia's primary intelligence agency.” The GIP is Saudi Arabia’s foreign spy service. The DDoSecrets copy holds an org chart, a thirty-one-page station document, a list of 556 personnel, and hundreds of images. Who Dumped It The group presents itself as working with the cyber arm of Ansar Allah, the Houthis’ formal name. DDoSecrets says Uways Qarani is allegedly affiliated with the Houthis, the Iran-backed movement at war with Saudi Arabia. It added: “The data was flagged by Handala, which is alleged to have ties to Iranian intelligence.” That’s the claim. Not everyone buys it. The threat-intelligence firm StealthMole concluded the Houthi tie is “a claim the group makes, consistently and loudly, and nothing more can be confirmed.” The analysis firm SpecialEurasia raised the chance of “a proxy or cut-out supported by another cyber actor or state, with the Houthi identity providing political cover and attributional ambiguity.” StealthMole tracked the group for weeks. It wrote: “Each leak is presented as building on the last.” The hackers say they went further this time. StealthMole reports they claimed “the 500 officers had been matched against the Saudi water-subscriber data claimed the week before to find their homes.” Who actually runs the group is unknown. StealthMole wrote: “Uways Qarani itself is not designated, and nothing in its posts explains who runs it.” Why It Could Be Fake A leak from an enemy at war is a weapon. It can mix real names with planted ones to sow panic or frame innocent people. DDoSecrets warns that with cyberwar data “there is an increased chance of malware, ulterior motives and altered or implanted data, or false flags/fake personas.” Dark Web Informer wrote: “The authenticity, completeness, source and current availability of the claimed dataset have not been independently verified.” Undercode News said “the material should be treated as an unverified threat-actor claim, rather than a confirmed breach.” SpecialEurasia warned that “it is not currently possible to independently corroborate the identity, employment status or contact details of these individuals.” A Map of Saudi Spying The station document opens with an index. It splits Saudi intelligence work into five regions: Asia, Europe, Africa, the Americas, and Oceania. Index page of the station document, as released by DDoSecrets. It lists no personal names. Asia dominates, with offices tied to Iran, Syria, Jordan, Bahrain, and Indonesia. Europe includes a separate section for Britain. The Americas section covers a Washington office. The pages look like slides built from source files, not raw internal records. That fits a group out to make a splash. Friends Get Burned Too Spy services trade secrets through liaison, an official channel between friendly agencies. Each side names a liaison officer as its point of contact. An attaché is an officer posted openly to an embassy. The station file is built around that channel. Every page carries the heading “Offices and External Liaison” (المكاتب والارتباط الخارجي). Dozens of cards name partner nations’ liaison officers. They include a German liaison officer (ضابط الاتصال الألماني), a British station director (مدير المحطة البريطانية), and a Yemeni liaison officer, National Security (ضابط الاتصال اليمني (الأمن القومي)). Diplomatic titles show up too: a Qatar attaché office (ملحقية قطر), an embassy secretary in Indonesia (سكرتير السفارة في إندونيسيا), and a consul at the Saudi embassy in Jordan (قنصل سفارة السعودية بالأردن). Declared liaisons were never secret to their hosts. But now any hostile service can see which of America’s and Europe’s spy agencies talk to Riyadh, and through whom. The hackers claimed more. StealthMole reports their first post “accused them of working with Mossad and the UAE under forged diplomatic cover.” The files show no proof of that. The Collaborators and the Drivers Every spy service runs on sources, people who pass secrets to an officer. Stations also hire locals, such as drivers and fixers, who see where officers go and whom they meet. The files never use the word source. But two cards on the Syria pages are titled Syrian collaborator (متعاون سوري), next to a Syrian file management team (فريق إدارة الملف السوري). Other cards list a Pakistani driver (سواق باكستاني), drivers for the Sudanese liaison officer (سواق ضابط الاتصال السوداني), and a Sudanese, for camp rentals (سوداني لتأجير المخيمات) contact. The files don’t say whether a collaborator is a paid source or a volunteer. SpecialEurasia said only that the material “appears to associate individuals with contact information and organisational functions.” These are the people with the least protection. An officer has a passport and a government behind him. A collaborator in a war zone has only his anonymity, and this leak prints his phone number. Minutes to a Home Address OctoProbe ran two people the document places in its Washington office through its identifier graph, a map of how phone numbers, emails, and accounts connect. In about sixteen minutes, the trail ran from the leaked phone numbers to home addresses in Northern Virginia, license plates, and Washington-area phone lines. It also turned up a language-learning profile, a check-in app account, a Telegram handle, and a LinkedIn page. Relatives’ names and birth dates came along for the ride. OctoProbe investigation graph. Click to zoom. That is what an adversary can do with this list. Find the house. Find the car. Follow the officer to the source. Reviews That Put Them in Riyadh Email accounts tied to the leaked contacts left a trail on Google Maps. OctoProbe logged fifteen location observations from Google Maps reviews linked to those emails. The visible reviews run from October 2021 to August 2026. All but one are in Riyadh: Hittin, Olaya Street, Ar Rabi (three times), Alhazm, and Shubra. The outlier is a restaurant in Istanbul, reviewed in October 2025. Most of the activity falls in the last eighteen months. Google Maps reviews tied to the investigation’s email accounts, mapped by OctoProbe. That corroborates a large part of the leak’s Saudi footprint. It does not verify the files. But it shows one more trail that cover can’t hide: a restaurant review, posted from a linked account, pins its author to a neighborhood. Cover Doesn’t Last Spies depend on cover, a false or limited identity that hides their real job. They guard it with operational security (OPSEC), habits that keep enemies from learning what they do. That worked when the trail was paper. Now one phone number links to a carrier, a car, an address history, and a dozen apps. Human intelligence (HUMINT), spying through people instead of machines, still matters. Officers still meet sources face to face. But the officer carries a phone that never stops talking. Once a leak ties his name to that number, his cover is gone in an afternoon, and his sources are next. Bottom Line Confidence: The release is real. Whether every name is genuine is unproven. The Northern Virginia link carries moderate confidence; the risk to anyone named is high either way. Method: OctoProbe read the DDoSecrets index, the station PDF (Arabic titles transcribed from page images and linked by page), the personnel file, and the reports linked above, then expanded identifiers on October 16, 2026. Disclaimer This is an analytic assessment of leaked material released by a hostile group. The documents are unverified, and no one has been shown to be an intelligence officer.

posts.title: Whose Coffee? An Anti-Bot Developer’s Handle Turns Up on Archive.today’s Donate Link
posts.description: An anti-bot developer known as glizzykingdreko runs Takion API, a commercial bot-check bypass service. His donation page appeared in Archive.today’s donate link from August 2025 to October 2026. He now disclaims any tie.
posts.body: Cover. Cartoon avatar from the public glizzykingdreko profiles. Map of Medellín, Colombia, the city of the persona’s one public Google Maps review. Map © OpenStreetMap contributors. The finding: Archive.today, the anonymous web-archiving site the FBI is trying to unmask, pointed its “donate” button at the personal donation page of an Italian anti-bot developer known online as glizzy (@glizzykingdreko). That page links to his company, Takion API. Takion sells a service that defeats website bot checks. Archived copies of Archive.today’s homepage show the link from August 2025 through at least October 4, 2026. We assess it is likely that Takion’s owner has a working relationship with Archive.today’s donation setup. We do not find evidence that he runs Archive.today. In September 2026 he added a notice to his donation page denying any connection to “third-party archiving services or web mirrors.” Key Findings Persona and company are one operation (high confidence). The glizzykingdreko donation page calls Takion’s blog “My company blog.” Takion’s website lists his GitHub projects as its own research. The handle sat in Archive.today’s donate link (high confidence). Wayback Machine copies of Archive.ph from August 1, 2025, to October 4, 2026, show the donate button pointing to buymeacoffee.com/glizzykingdreko. Other copies point to Archive.today’s own Liberapay page and to three other donation handles. Takion is tied to Archive.today’s donation money (likely). His supporter count rose from 14 to 177 while the link ran. We cannot see who paid or why. Takion powers Archive.today (unproven). Takion sells exactly the bot-check bypass a mass web archiver needs. We found no technical link between Takion and Archive.today’s servers. Takion is the commercial end of paywall-bypass infrastructure (low confidence). Takion markets scraping, not paywall bypass. This rests on the donation link alone. Locations. Italy: high confidence, from three platforms. Germany: low confidence, through a separate “kingdreko” identity tied in only by handle similarity. Medellín, Colombia: high confidence that the account reviewed a shop there, about a year ago. What Takion API Sells Takion API is an anti-bot bypass service. It is a paid tool that gets automated scrapers past the checks websites use to block bots (a bypass API). Its homepage says: “One POST returns fresh cookies, headers, and sensor tokens to scrape data through Cloudflare, DataDome, PerimeterX, Imperva, and more.” In plain terms, a customer sends one request and gets back the credentials a real browser would earn. The site also says “We are the only team publishing antibot research in the open: DataDome solvers, Akamai sensor encryption, captcha deobfuscators.” Those projects sit on the glizzykingdreko GitHub account, which hosts 77 public repositories. Most of the top-starred ones are tools that break DataDome, Akamai, PerimeterX, and hCaptcha bot checks. His BrowJect library calls Takion “the best antibot bypass API provider”. SecurityTrails lists 65 subdomains of takionapi.tech, many named for bot-check vendors and target sites, mostly hosted at Hostinger. Screenshot via OctoProbe. The subdomains tell the same story. SecurityTrails, a DNS history service, lists sixty-five of them. Many are named for the systems Takion defeats, including incapsula, hcaptcha, geetest, forter, px-web, nudata, and 2captcha. Others carry the names of target sites such as stubhub and airbnb. The main domain sits behind Cloudflare, with mail at Proton. The OctoProbe graph’s DNS records show the same Cloudflare name servers and Proton mail servers. One Persona, Several Handles The glizzy persona uses one name across platforms. X, @glizzykingdreko: joined January 2022, “Account based in Italy,” verified since June 2026, two username changes, connected through the Italy App Store. X, @TakionAPI: joined February 2024, “Account based in Italy.” Instagram, glizzykingdreko: country IT, created January 1, 2022, with earlier usernames glyzzikingdreko and glyzzykingdreko. GitHub, glizzykingdreko: created January 10, 2022. The bio is Latin: “Per aspera ad astra.” X “About this account” pages. Left: @glizzykingdreko, based in Italy, joined January 2022. Right: @TakionAPI, based in Italy, joined February 2024. Screenshots via OctoProbe. Instagram lookup for glizzykingdreko: country IT, earlier usernames glyzzikingdreko and glyzzykingdreko. Email hint and numeric ID masked by OctoProbe. The Donate Button This is the central evidence. Archive.today’s homepage has a small “donate” link in its header. The Internet Archive’s Wayback Machine has saved the page many times, and each saved copy keeps the link’s target. Before August 2025: The link pointed to Archive.today’s own pages, buymeacoffee.com/archive.today (2023 to 2024) and liberapay.com/archiveis. May to July 2025: Monthly copies show two other donation handles, jotarokujo and philipdwyer. From August 1, 2025: Copies begin pointing to buymeacoffee.com/glizzykingdreko. Later hits include December 1, 2025, March 1, 2026, and October 4, 2026. One October 2025 copy shows a fourth handle, watersucks. Rotation: The target changes from day to day. A copy from October 3, 2026 shows Liberapay. The next day’s shows glizzykingdreko. In a sample of 91 copies from April 2025 to October 2026, 68 pointed to Liberapay and 20 to glizzykingdreko. Archive.ph homepage as saved by the Wayback Machine on October 4, 2026. In that copy’s source, the “donate” link goes to buymeacoffee.com/glizzykingdreko. The glizzykingdreko donation page grew while the link ran. Saved copies show 14 supporters on August 4, 2025, 56 in December 2025, 126 in March 2026, 167 in July 2026, and 177 by mid-September 2026. The live page showed 181 on October 15, 2026. The page links to Takion’s blog as “My company blog.” Then the page changed. A copy from September 10, 2026, has no disclaimer. A copy from September 14 has this one: This is my personal creator page. I have absolutely NO affiliation, partnership, or connection with any third-party archiving services or web mirrors. Any placement or embedding of this link on external websites without my explicit written consent is completely unauthorized — Glizzy, buymeacoffee.com/glizzykingdreko The glizzykingdreko donation page on October 15, 2026, with its September 2026 disclaimer. Contact email withheld by OctoProbe. Assessment. Two readings fit the record. In the first, Archive.today’s operator sent donations to a supplier or partner, and the disclaimer came after the link drew attention. In the second, Archive.today chose his page without his consent, as the disclaimer says. The second reading leaves gaps. The link ran for more than a year, and the page added supporters the whole time. It also sat next to other one-off handles, which looks like a deliberate list. We rate the working relationship likely, not confirmed. Only payment records would settle it. The FBI Subpoena The FBI is trying to learn who runs Archive.today. In fall 2025, it subpoenaed Tucows, the Canadian registrar of the site’s domain. The Verge reported: “The FBI is attempting to track down the identity of the owner of Archive.today and its numerous mirrors”. The subpoena demanded the “customer or subscriber name, address of service, and billing address”, The Verge said. It added that the order states the information “relates to a federal criminal investigation being conducted by the FBI”. Ars Technica wrote that the FBI sought “subscriber information on [the] customer behind archive.today”. It also noted that “its registrant “Denis Petrov” may be an alias”. The German outlet heise online reported the subpoena on November 5, 2025. It cited a 2023 analysis finding that “Archive.today uses a botnet with changing IP addresses to circumvent anti-scraping measures”. heise added: “Whether the court order is genuine and how the operators of the site obtained it could not be verified so far.” Archive.today’s own FAQ says: “It is privately funded; there are no complex finances behind it.” How it bears on Takion. The subpoena seeks payment records, and donations are payment records. A donate link that routes money to an outside developer’s page is the kind of trail such a subpoena could follow. heise’s cited botnet claim describes the problem Takion sells a fix for: getting past anti-scraping walls at scale. That is a fit in motive and capability, not evidence of a contract. Nothing in the reporting names glizzy, Takion, or any Italian operator. Where Archive.today Is Hosted SecurityTrails, a domain-records service owned by Recorded Future, lists FranTech Solutions as the hosting provider for Archive.today and for every subdomain it shows, more than 10,000 in all. It lists Tutao GmbH, the German company behind the Tuta encrypted email service, as the mail provider. SecurityTrails lists FranTech Solutions as the hosting provider for Archive.today and its subdomains, with Tutao GmbH as the mail provider. Account details cropped out. Via OctoProbe. Our own check on October 16, 2026, shows a more layered setup. Archive.today and Archive.ph point to two internet addresses, 104.36.80.106 and 104.36.80.107. The mirrors Archive.is, Archive.md, Archive.li, Archive.vn and Archive.fo use the same pair. The American Registry for Internet Numbers lists that address block under IncogNet LLC. IncogNet’s network number, or ASN (the ID a network uses to route traffic on the internet), is AS40663. Routing data from RIPE NCC, the European internet registry, shows FranTech’s network, AS53667, as one of IncogNet’s direct links to the wider internet. FranTech sells servers under the BuyVM brand. Archive.today’s mail still runs through Tuta. FranTech has drawn scrutiny before. In 2019, TechRadar reported that research by the security firm Bromium found that “malicious threats were originating from web servers in Las Vegas, Nevada registered under the name PONYNET and hosted on BuyVM data centers.” PONYNET is the registered name of FranTech’s network. FranTech describes its own stance in BuyVM’s acceptable use policy: “Frantech is a strong believer and supporter of Freedom of Speech and has taken a strong, and in some cases very public, stance against censorship.” How it bears on Takion. Hosting records do not show who runs a site. They do place Archive.today on infrastructure that SecurityTrails ties to FranTech, a provider that by its own account takes a hands-off stance on content. Nothing in the hosting records names glizzy or Takion. The Medellín Google Maps Review The OctoProbe graph links the persona’s email to a Google Maps contributor profile. The profile name is “Glizzy KingDreko.” It holds one public review, of an action-camera shop in Medellín, Colombia. Google dates it “a year ago” as of October 15, 2026, so roughly late 2025. Google says the review was written in Italian, and the shop replied in Spanish. Google Maps contributor profile “Glizzy KingDreko,” a Local Guide Level 2. Its one review gives The House Technology, a shop in the Laureles–Estadio area of Medellín, Colombia, five stars and is dated “a year ago.” Google translated the review from Italian. Street number masked by OctoProbe. What it implies. The Italian-language review matches the Italy signals on X, Instagram, and the App Store. A camera-shop visit points to travel or a stay in Medellín around late 2025, during the donate-link period. It does not show where he lives now. Medellín is a common base for remote workers, and one review is one data point. Italy and Germany Italy (high confidence). Both X accounts say “based in Italy.” The personal X account connects through the Italy App Store. Instagram reports country IT. The Maps review is in Italian. Germany (low confidence). The graph holds a second cluster under the shorter handle “kingdreko” and a related “d.italiano” handle. That cluster has German-domain email addresses (k***@gmx.de, d.i***@hotmail.de, d***@msn.de) and a username hit on the Eintracht Frankfurt fan-community site. Data records link those addresses to one real name, which we withhold. The link to glizzy is only an analyst’s seed (a starting identifier entered by hand), based on the shared “kingdreko” string. No record in the graph ties the two clusters together. The Germany thread is a lead, not a finding. Identifier Graph OctoProbe identifier graph for this investigation (480 nodes, 591 edges), exported with privacy mode on. The graph has 480 nodes and 591 links across twenty-two expansion rounds. Most nodes are noise from common handles such as “glizzy” and “d.” The table below keeps the ones that carry weight. Identifier Type Source Links to Supports g***@protonmail.com Email Seed; OSINT modules glizzykingdreko username, GitHub, Gravatar, Maps profile Persona hub glizzykingdreko Username Seed; OSINT, Instagram X, Instagram, GitHub, Medium, Buy Me a Coffee One persona across platforms takionapi.tech Domain Seed; DNS, WHOIS Cloudflare name servers, Proton mail servers Takion hosting; WHOIS private takionapi (X, GitHub) Username Seed TakionAPI X account Company persona, Italy Maps contributor 1057… URL OSINT (Google Maps) via the persona email “Glizzy Kingdreko” name Medellín review in Italian webmaster@archive.ph Email Seed (analyst-added) Google account with an empty Maps profile No link to the persona found k***@gmx.de, d.i***@gmx.net Email Seed; data records kingdreko and d.italiano usernames, one withheld name Germany lead (low) community.eintracht.de profile URL OSINT via the d.italiano username d.italiano Germany lead (low) buymeacoffee.com/glizzykingdreko URL OSINT; Wayback Machine Archive.ph donate link; Takion blog Donation link (likely relationship) Evidence on the Archive.today Link Supports a relationship: Archive.today’s donate button pointed to the glizzykingdreko page in many saved copies over fourteen months. That page names Takion as the owner’s company. Supporters grew more than twelvefold while the link ran. Takion sells the bot-check bypass a mass archiver needs. Cuts against it, or remains unproven: The owner denies any connection in writing. The donate link rotated among Liberapay and at least four handles, so glizzy was one recipient of several. We found no shared server, IP address, or DNS record between takionapi.tech and Archive.today. The webmaster@archive.ph Google account shows no tie to the persona. Takion’s homepage, docs, and blog index never mention paywalls or Archive.today. Press coverage of the subpoena names no suspect. Method Sources: The investigation combined open-source collection with premium and proprietary data pulls across 30+ services. Cited public sources: Wayback Machine copies of Archive.ph and of the Buy Me a Coffee page, takionapi.tech, GitHub, The Verge, Ars Technica, heise online, Google Maps, and screenshots captured by OctoProbe. Emails, phone numbers, and account IDs are masked. Capture date: October 15, 2026. Disclaimer This is an analytic assessment of public information. Nobody named here has been charged with a crime in connection with Archive.today. “Likely” and “assessed” mark judgments, not established facts.

posts.title: Heather Zhang Case: OSINT Trail From a 2024 Reddit Allegation
posts.description: Charged, not convicted: Irvine realtor Wanying "Heather" Zhang is accused of acting as an unregistered PRC agent. An OctoProbe investigation began from a January 2024 Reddit allegation naming Fatai Miao, whom CBS News identifies as "Individual 1." DOJ has not accused him of wrongdoing.
posts.body: Cover. Photo of Wanying “Heather” Zhang released by the FBI, as published by CBS News. Zhang is charged, not convicted. Summary: OctoProbe's investigation did not start with Zhang. It started with a January 2024 Reddit post accusing a man named Fatai Miao of selling a fake Bahamian passport. On October 8, 2026, CBS News identified Miao as “Individual 1,” the unnamed companion in the federal complaint against Wanying “Heather” Zhang. The Justice Department charges that Zhang, 34, of Irvine, acted as an unregistered agent of the PRC and surveilled relatives of a high-ranking Taiwanese official in the Pacific Northwest on September 1, 2025. CBS reports the family lives in a Seattle suburb. Zhang is charged and presumed innocent. Miao is not charged, and DOJ has not accused him of wrongdoing. The Reddit claims are anonymous and unverified; they concern Miao alone, and the retrievable text of the post never names or describes Zhang. Key finding Storyline: The Reddit allegation named Miao. Seeding his public identifiers produced an Arcadia, CA address-and-business cluster. CBS separately reports that rental-car paperwork for the alleged Seattle trip listed an address in Arcadia. That overlap, at city level, is the link between the 2024 scam allegation and the 2026 case. Timeline: Reddit allegation (Jan 2024), then the alleged trip (Aug 29 to Sept 1, 2025), Miao's reported one-way flight to China (about two weeks before an Oct 7, 2026 hearing), Zhang's arrest at LAX (Sunday, Oct 4, 2026), and this investigation (opened Oct 8, 2026). Geography: Irvine and Arcadia are the two Southern California anchors. John Wayne Airport, Las Vegas, and the Seattle area make up the alleged 2025 route, and LAX is the arrest site. Confidence: High for the charging facts, which come from DOJ. Moderate for Miao as Individual 1, which rests on CBS reporting. Low for the Reddit claims, which are anonymous and uncorroborated. The alleged face match is unverified and is left to the reader. The case: what DOJ charges Per the DOJ press release, Zhang was “arrested Sunday on a one count complaint charging her with acting in the United States as an unregistered agent of the government of the People’s Republic of China (PRC)”. That Sunday was October 4, 2026. DOJ says “Zhang was arrested prior to her planned departure from Los Angeles International Airport, where she planned to board a flight to China.” The New York Post adds that she “was busted as she tried to board a flight to Shanghai.” The surveillance trip, per the complaint as summarized by DOJ: “On Aug. 29, 2025, Zhang and another individual flew from John Wayne Airport in Orange County to Las Vegas.” Then “On Sept. 1, 2025, they flew from Las Vegas to the Pacific Northwest, where the victims reside.” Once there: Upon their arrival, Zhang and the other individual traveled to the victims’ residence and conducted surveillance. — U.S. Department of Justice CBS News reports the target was Lai Ting-yu, son of Taiwan's president, and that the FBI cites “footage from a neighbor's security camera”. A federal judge ordered Zhang held as a flight risk at a detention hearing on Wednesday, October 7. The $190,000. CBS reports that prosecutor Amanda Elbogen “told the court Wednesday that Zhang had received $190,000 into a Chinese bank account” from a cryptocurrency exchange business. The New York Post describes it as “access to $190,000 in a secret Chinese cryptocurrency account”. The Post also reports a November 2023 photo of her behind an All American Chinese Association (AACA) banner during Xi Jinping's San Francisco visit. As DOJ itself notes, “A criminal complaint is merely an allegation.” “Individual 1”: what the press reports The complaint does not name Individual 1. CBS News identifies him as Fatai Miao: “Fatai Miao, a Chinese-born California construction entrepreneur, is the man believed to have accompanied realtor Wanying Zhang to Seattle in September 2025”. The identification rests on the FBI affidavit. CBS quotes the agent's statement that the rental paperwork listed a house he sold, as “Based on public records, I know that Individual 1 sold a house at this address on or about September 11, 2025”. The Taipei Times, relaying CBS, says the affidavit “contained clues that helped identify Miao as” Individual 1. The flight. CBS reports that Individual 1 “left on a one-way ticket to China about two weeks ago, prosecutors said during Wednesday's hearing.” FBI agents searched his empty Irvine home on Sunday, October 4. CBS is explicit: “The Justice Department has not accused him of any wrongdoing”, and a relative described him as a “follower.” The New York Post, citing sources, describes Miao as Zhang's lover. Miao is not charged with any crime. Where the trail started: the Reddit passport-scam allegation The investigation's starting lead was “Fake Bahamian passport scam,” r/Scams, posted January 14, 2024 by an anonymous user. What the poster alleges, in their own words: Who: The poster names “Mr FATAI MIAO” and says Miao claimed a relative (a nephew, named in the post) was a Bahamian official posted to Ghana who “could help me apply for a Bahamian passport and ID for a fee of US$300,000”. The post lists a phone number for that relative; we withhold it. Money and payment method: The poster wrote that they “made the first payment of 60,000 USDT” and that “a total of 305,000 USDT was transferred to him”. USDT is the Tether stablecoin. The passport and Malaysia: The poster wrote that the passport was mailed to Dubai and that on June 1, 2023, “I was investigated by the local customs and was detained with a fake traveling document”. Scale and claimed insiders: The poster wrote that “someone within the Bahamas Immigration Bureau has processed more than 70 such passports”, and described screenshots of “The chats where he pretended to be a Bahamian official to deceive me.” Companies: The retrieved text names no company. A commenter offered the plainest reading: “You ran into a counterfeiter and essentially bought a fake passport.” Assessment. The post is a single anonymous account. Its exhibits (the passport, chats and a claimed immigration certificate) are only what the poster says they uploaded. Nothing here verifies the payments, the Malaysian detention or any Bahamian insider, and the account fits a counterfeit-document sale at least as well as an insider scheme. The post's only point of contact with the DOJ case is the name Fatai Miao. It predates the alleged trip by 19 months and does not mention Zhang, Taiwan, surveillance or the PRC. The connection comes from CBS identifying Miao as Individual 1, together with the city-level Arcadia overlap described below. It does not come from anything in the post. Ludepress reaches the same conclusion: “两条线索目前能够确认的交集，仅在于公开资料均提到了名为Fatai Miao的人物。” In our translation, that says the only confirmable intersection is that public records on both threads mention a person named Fatai Miao. Ludepress also writes “目前尚无独立证据证实这些指控”, which translates as “there is currently no independent evidence confirming these allegations.” Sourcing note: Reddit blocks automated access, and archived copies contain no post text. The Reddit quotes above are taken verbatim from a search-engine index copy of the post, retrieved October 15, 2026, and could not be checked against the live page. The figure below shows the Chinese-language outlet Ludepress, which summarized the post on October 12, 2026 and itself notes that there is no independent evidence for the claims and no public evidence tying them to the Zhang case. Secondary coverage of the Reddit allegation: Ludepress, Oct 12, 2026, captured October 15, 2026. Original post: reddit.com/r/Scams. The claims are unverified, and Miao is not charged. OSINT analysis Identifier graph The investigation was opened on October 8, 2026 with five seed identifiers. After 11 rounds and 123 queries, it holds 221 nodes and 545 edges, including 58 addresses, 20 phone numbers, 10 email addresses, 15 usernames, 22 profile URLs, and 19 corporate entities. The Reddit thread is a node in the graph, attached to a subject cluster built around an Arcadia, CA address, several phone numbers and email addresses (all withheld), and construction and real-estate business registrations. The investigation also holds three images that were manually uploaded from the Reddit post, plus three images taken from a Chinese-language company website, which are attached to a separate subject. OctoProbe identifier graph for the investigation (221 nodes, 545 edges), exported from the app with privacy mode on. Addresses, phone numbers, and emails are redacted. Alleged close match: Reddit license photo vs. HenHexin image The Reddit thread includes a photo of a California driver license in the name of Fatai Miao, posted publicly by the anonymous poster. Separately, the investigation holds an image published on henghexin.com showing a man in a suit at a desk with Chinese Communist Party flags; that setting is as published by HenHexin. The two images are presented here as an alleged close match. OctoProbe does not say they show the same person, makes no claim about party membership, and leaves the conclusion to the reader. Miao is not charged with any crime. A: License image posted publicly by an anonymous r/Scams user in the “Fake Bahamian passport scam” thread. License number, street address, ZIP, date of birth, expiration, document numbers and signature redacted by OctoProbe. B: Image as published by HenHexin at henghexin.com/party/detail?id=57 (original file). The CCP-flag setting is as published there. OctoProbe makes no claim about the person's identity or affiliations. Side-by-side face crops of A (Reddit license photo) and B (henghexin.com image), presented as an alleged close match. Readers can draw their own conclusions; OctoProbe does not assert that they are the same person. Timeline Jun 1, 2023: The Reddit poster says they were detained in Malaysia with the passport (claim not verified). Nov 2023: A photo shows Zhang behind an AACA banner during Xi's San Francisco visit (NY Post, CBS). Jan 14, 2024: The r/Scams post naming Fatai Miao is published. Aug 29, 2025: Zhang allegedly flies from John Wayne Airport to Las Vegas (DOJ). Sep 1, 2025: Alleged surveillance in the Seattle area. CBS reports that Individual 1 was in the rented SUV. About two weeks before Oct 7, 2026: Miao takes a one-way flight to China, per prosecutors as reported by CBS. Sun, Oct 4, 2026: Zhang is arrested at LAX trying to board a flight to Shanghai, and the FBI searches Miao's empty Irvine home (CBS). Mon, Oct 5, 2026: DOJ announces the charge; Zhang makes her initial court appearance (DOJ, CBS). Wed, Oct 7, 2026: Detention hearing; the judge orders Zhang held as a flight risk (CBS). Thu, Oct 8, 2026: CBS identifies Miao as Individual 1, and the OctoProbe investigation opens. Oct 9 to 12, 2026: NY Post (Oct 9), Taipei Times (Oct 10), and Ludepress (Oct 12) coverage. Oct 19, 2026: Zhang's next court date (NY Post). Geography The pattern of life clusters in two Southern California cities about 34 miles apart in a straight line (about 40 miles, or roughly an hour, by road). Irvine is Zhang's city of residence (DOJ) and the site of Miao's searched home (CBS). Arcadia is the city CBS says appeared on the rental paperwork, and it is also where the graph's address-and-business cluster sits. The alleged 2025 route ran from John Wayne Airport, about 2.5 miles from central Irvine in a straight line (about a 10-minute drive), to Las Vegas and then to the Seattle area. The arrest happened at LAX. All locations are shown at city or venue level. No home locations are shown. Pattern of life at city and venue level, compiled from DOJ, CBS News, and the OctoProbe graph. Map data © OpenStreetMap contributors. No residential addresses are shown. Confidence High: Zhang's charge, arrest, and alleged travel dates, from DOJ's own release. Moderate: Miao as Individual 1, which comes from CBS reporting and documents and is not stated by DOJ. The Arcadia overlap is also moderate: it holds at city level only. Low: The Reddit passport claims, which are anonymous and uncorroborated, and the reported romantic relationship, which rests on unnamed sources in the NY Post. Unassessed: The alleged close match between the Reddit license photo and the HenHexin image. OctoProbe draws no conclusion. Method Sources: The investigation combined open-source collection with premium and proprietary data pulls across 30+ services. Sources cited here: the DOJ press release, CBS News, the New York Post, the Taipei Times, Ludepress, the public Reddit thread, and the OctoProbe identifier graph. Phone numbers, email addresses, and street numbers are withheld. Capture date: October 15, 2026. Disclaimer Zhang is charged in a federal criminal complaint; Miao is not charged. A criminal complaint or indictment is an accusation, not proof; every defendant is presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty in a court of law.

posts.title: Christopher W. Burns: Public Google Maps Activity Dated After His Last Sighting, Wayne, PA Area
posts.description: A Maps account allegedly attributed to Burns shows Wayne and Wynnewood, PA activity (~2021, ~2023) after his September 24, 2020 last sighting.
posts.body: Summary: A Google Maps contributor account allegedly attributed to Christopher W. Burns shows activity in the Wayne, PA area after the FBI's last known sighting. The FBI says Burns "has not been seen since he left his home on September 24, 2020." The "Chris Burns" profile, which OctoProbe's identifier graph ties to Burns's name variants and personal email, carries a review at PrimoHoagies in Wayne dated "5 years ago" (~2021) and a rating at Target in Wynnewood dated "3 years ago" (~2023). Both sites sit on the Lancaster Avenue / Main Line corridor, roughly 7 miles apart, in the same area as Burns's FBI-listed birthplace and the Wayne addresses and employer in his identifier graph. Assessment: moderate-confidence indicator of post-flight presence on the Philadelphia Main Line, strongest for the ~2023 data point. Key finding Timeline: FBI last sighting September 24, 2020 (Georgia). Maps activity ~2021 (Wayne) and ~2023 (Wynnewood). Both fall after the disappearance. Geography: PrimoHoagies (Wayne) and Target (Wynnewood) are about 7 miles apart on the same Lancaster Avenue corridor, inside the Main Line area where his birthplace, two graph addresses, and a linked employer also sit. Indication: Repeat, everyday consumer activity (food, retail) in his home region, spaced about two years apart, is consistent with residence or recurring presence on the Main Line rather than a one-off pass-through. Confidence: Moderate. The account links to Burns through shared identifiers in the graph; the ~2023 rating is the stronger timing signal because the ~2021 review sits closer to the 2020 boundary once Google's rounding is applied. FBI public information From the FBI Most Wanted Fraudsters page for Christopher W. Burns, viewed October 15, 2026: Charge: Mail fraud. A federal arrest warrant was issued October 23, 2020, in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Georgia (Atlanta). Alleged conduct: Burns allegedly defrauded dozens of victims of at least $10 million through a purported "peer to peer" lending program secured by collateral that did not exist or was worth substantially less than represented. Last seen: September 24, 2020, when he left his home, one day before he was due to provide business documents to the SEC. His vehicle was later found abandoned in Dunwoody, Georgia. Last known residence: Berkeley Lake, Georgia. Description: Date of birth used December 11, 1982. Place of birth Wayne, Pennsylvania. 6'2", about 240 lb, brown hair, brown eyes. Tattoo of three interlaced black triangles on the left forearm. Former Registered Investment Advisor. Reward: Up to $150,000. FBI Most Wanted Fraudsters page for Christopher W. Burns, captured October 15, 2026. Source: fbi.gov. OSINT analysis Identifier graph Starting from public identifiers, OctoProbe built a graph of 25 nodes and 47 edges connecting the FBI wanted page to: Name variants: Christopher Burns, Chris Burns, Christopher L Burns Two Wayne, PA addresses (street numbers withheld) Two email addresses (one personal ISP address, one corporate) and two phone numbers, all withheld An organization: a Wayne-area pharmaceutical company, linked through the corporate email, phone, and address Five usernames and six profile URLs: LinkedIn, Foursquare, Pandora, Myspace, and a Google Maps contributor profile OctoProbe identifier graph for Burns: 25 nodes, 47 edges, centered on the Wayne, PA cluster. Privacy Mode on. Google Maps contributor activity The "Chris Burns" profile (Local Guide Level 2, 1 review, 1 rating) sits in the same graph cluster as Burns's name variants and personal email: Google Maps contributor profile. Captured October 15, 2026: Place Contribution Date shown by Google Approx. year After Sep 24, 2020? PrimoHoagies, Wayne, PA 1-star review (owner reply also "5 years ago") "5 years ago" ~2021 Yes Target, Wynnewood, PA (Lancaster Ave corridor) 1-star rating "3 years ago" ~2023 Yes Timeline Sep 24, 2020: Burns leaves his home in Berkeley Lake, GA; vehicle later found abandoned in Dunwoody, GA. Oct 23, 2020: Federal arrest warrant issued (N.D. Georgia). ~2021: Review posted at PrimoHoagies, Wayne, PA, with an owner reply from the same period. ~2023: Rating posted at Target, Wynnewood, PA. Geography Both sites sit on the Lancaster Avenue (Main Line) corridor west of Philadelphia, about 7 miles apart. Wayne is Burns's FBI-listed birthplace, and the graph's two addresses and linked employer are also in the Wayne area. The post-2020 activity lands in the same tight cluster as his pre-flight footprint, not in Georgia. Google Maps contributor profile “Chris Burns,” captured October 15, 2026: Wayne (~2021) and Wynnewood (~2023) contributions, both after the September 24, 2020 last sighting. Method Sources: The FBI wanted page, the public Google Maps contributor profile, and other public profile pages, correlated into an OctoProbe identifier graph. Capture date: October 15, 2026.
